chapters.n: Matthew opens his Gospel by presenting Jesus’s family line. Writing especially for Jewish readers, he shows that Jesus is the heir of the two great covenants: the royal promise to David and the blessing promised to Abraham.

f.g: Genealogy, origin — the Greek word is genesis.

chapters.n: The line begins with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “Judas” is the Greek form of Judah, the son through whom the royal line would come.

f.g: Judah, son of Jacob — Greek forms of Old Testament names are used throughout.
Fathered, or became ancestor of.

chapters.n: Matthew unusually includes women. Tamar, a Canaanite widow, bore twins to Judah after a troubled episode. Including her shows God working through imperfect family stories.

f.g: Perez and Zerah, Judah’s twin sons.
Hezron.

chapters.n: The list continues through the generations in Egypt and the wilderness. Nahshon was the leader of Judah’s tribe in Moses’s day.

f.g: Ram (1 Chronicles 2:9-10).
Nahshon, Aaron’s brother-in-law.

chapters.n: Two more remarkable women: Rahab, the Canaanite of Jericho who protected Israel’s spies, and Ruth, the Moabite who chose Israel’s God. Gentile women are part of the Messiah’s heritage.

f.g: Rahab.
Boaz.

chapters.n: David becomes king. Matthew pointedly calls Bathsheba “the wife of Uriah,” recalling David’s sin — and God’s grace in continuing the line through Solomon.

f.w: her that had been the wife of Urias

chapters.n: After Solomon come the kings of Judah: Rehoboam, Abijah, and Asa.

f.g: Rehoboam, under whom the kingdom split.
Abijah (Abijam).

chapters.n: Next are Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Uzziah. Matthew skips three kings between Jehoram and Uzziah — ancient genealogies often abbreviated to make a pattern.

f.g: Jehoshaphat, a righteous king.
Uzziah — Matthew omits Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah.

chapters.n: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — kings during Isaiah’s ministry.

f.g: Ahaz.
Hezekiah.

chapters.n: Manasseh, the most wicked king, who later repented; then Amon and the righteous reformer Josiah.

f.g: Josiah.

chapters.n: The Babylonian exile interrupts the royal line. “Jechonias” is Jehoiachin, actually Josiah’s grandson. The line of kings seems to end in disaster.

f.g: Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin or Coniah.

chapters.n: Yet the line continues in exile. Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin’s grandson, led the return from Babylon and rebuilt the temple.

f.g: Shealtiel.
Zerubbabel, governor of Judah.

chapters.n: From here the names aren’t found in the Old Testament; Matthew likely drew on family or public records. David’s descendants lived as ordinary people for centuries.

f.g: This and the following names appear only here.

chapters.n: More generations pass in obscurity, yet God preserved the line.

f.g: Zadok — not the famous priest of David’s time.

chapters.n: The list approaches Joseph. Luke 3 gives a different genealogy, which many explain as Mary’s line or a legal versus biological line.
Matthew carefully changes the pattern: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus.” Joseph was Jesus’s legal father, giving Him a royal claim, but Jesus was not his biological son.

f.g: Greek Christos, “Anointed One” — the same meaning as the Hebrew Messiah.

chapters.n: Matthew arranges the history into three sets of fourteen generations. Fourteen may echo David’s name, whose Hebrew letters add up to fourteen. History moves according to God’s plan toward Christ.

f.g: The Hebrew letters of David (D-W-D) have numeric values 4+6+4 = 14.

chapters.n: Mary was betrothed (legally pledged) to Joseph, but before they lived together she was found to be pregnant by the power of the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Betrothed — a binding engagement, legally like marriage, before the couple lived together.

f.w: with child of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Joseph, a righteous man, didn’t want to shame Mary publicly, so he planned to end the betrothal quietly. His goodness shows both obedience to the law and mercy.

f.g: Righteous, upright.
Divorce her privately; ending a betrothal required a divorce.

chapters.n: As Joseph considered this, an angel came in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take Mary as your wife; the child is from the Holy Ghost.” God guides Joseph through dreams, like the Joseph of Genesis.

f.g: A reminder of Joseph’s royal lineage, passed legally to Jesus.

chapters.n: Mary will have a son, and Joseph is to name Him Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins. The name itself declares His mission.

f.g: Greek form of Joshua (Yehoshua), meaning “Jehovah saves.”

f.w: he shall save his people from their sins

chapters.n: Matthew often notes how events fulfill prophecy — about a dozen times. This is the first.

f.g: A key phrase in Matthew, connecting Jesus to Old Testament prophecy.

chapters.n: Matthew quotes Isaiah: a virgin will bear a son called Emmanuel, “God with us.” In Jesus, God Himself came to live among His people.

f.w: Behold, a virgin shall be with child

f.g: Hebrew Immanu-El, “God with us.”

chapters.n: Joseph woke up and obeyed immediately, taking Mary as his wife. His quiet faith is an example of trusting revelation.

f.w: did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him

chapters.n: Joseph did not have marital relations with Mary until after Jesus’s birth, confirming the virgin birth. He named the child Jesus, as commanded, accepting Him as his legal son.

f.g: Did not have marital relations with her.

chapters.n: Jesus was born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. Wise men from the east — likely Persia or Babylonia — arrived in Jerusalem seeking Him.

f.g: Herod the Great, appointed king of Judea by Rome; infamous for cruelty.
Greek magoi — scholars of the stars from the east, perhaps Persian priests or astronomers.

chapters.n: They ask, “Where is the one born King of the Jews? We saw His star rise and came to worship Him.” Samuel the Lamanite also prophesied a new star at Christ’s birth.

f.g: JST reads “Where is the child that is born, the Messiah of the Jews?”

chapters.n: King Herod was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him. Herod jealously guarded his throne and had executed even his own family members.

f.g: Deeply disturbed, agitated.

chapters.n: Herod gathered the chief priests and scribes and asked where the Messiah was to be born. The religious experts knew the answer from scripture.

f.g: Experts in copying and interpreting the law of Moses.
The Messiah, the Anointed One.

chapters.n: They answered: in Bethlehem of Judea, as the prophet wrote.

f.g: Micah.

chapters.n: They quote Micah: from little Bethlehem will come a ruler who will shepherd God’s people Israel. Matthew blends Micah’s words with God’s promise to David to “feed my people.”

f.g: Ruler, leader.
Shepherd, tend.

chapters.n: Herod secretly called the wise men and carefully found out when the star first appeared, already plotting.

f.g: Privately, secretly.

chapters.n: He sent them to Bethlehem: “Find the child and report back, so I can worship Him too.” His “worship” was a lie to cover murder.

f.w: that I may come and worship him also
f.g: A deceptive pretext; his real aim appears in verse 16.

chapters.n: The star led them on to the place where the young child was. God guided seekers from afar.

f.w: stood over where the young child was
f.g: The star marked the exact location.

chapters.n: When they saw the star again, they were overjoyed — Matthew piles up words to show their joy.

f.g: Literally “rejoiced a great joy exceedingly.”

chapters.n: Entering the house, they found the young child with Mary, bowed down, and worshiped Him. They gave gold (for a king), frankincense (for worship of God), and myrrh (for burial), gifts often seen as symbols of who He is.

f.g: By now the family lived in a house; Jesus was a “young child,” perhaps up to two years old.
A fragrant resin burned as incense in worship.
A costly resin used in perfumes and burial.

chapters.n: Warned by God in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.

f.w: warned of God in a dream

chapters.n: Once they left, an angel told Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt with the child and Mary, because Herod wanted to kill Him. Egypt had long been a refuge for Israelites.
Joseph got up that very night and fled with them to Egypt. His prompt obedience saved the Savior’s life.

f.g: Without delay.

chapters.n: They stayed there until Herod died. Matthew sees Hosea’s words fulfilled: “Out of Egypt have I called my son.” As Israel was God’s son brought out of Egypt, so Jesus relives Israel’s story.

f.w: Out of Egypt have I called my son

chapters.n: Furious at being outwitted, Herod ordered all boys two and under in and around Bethlehem killed. Bethlehem was a small village, so perhaps a few dozen children died — a tragedy typical of Herod’s brutality.

f.g: Tricked, outwitted.
Surrounding districts.

chapters.n: This fulfilled words of Jeremiah.

f.g: Jeremiah.

chapters.n: Rachel, Israel’s ancestral mother buried near Bethlehem, is pictured weeping for her lost children. Jeremiah’s original verse is followed by a promise of hope and return.

f.g: Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem where exiles gathered.

chapters.n: After Herod died, an angel again appeared to Joseph in a dream in Egypt.

f.g: Herod died in about 4 BC.

chapters.n: “Get up and take the child and His mother back to Israel; those who sought His life are dead.” The words echo God’s command to Moses to return to Egypt.

f.w: they are dead which sought the young child's life

chapters.n: Joseph obeyed and returned with them to the land of Israel.

f.g: Joseph’s pattern: hear, rise, obey.

chapters.n: But Herod’s son Archelaus was ruling Judea, and Joseph feared him. Warned in another dream, he went to Galilee instead. Archelaus was so harsh that Rome removed him in AD 6.

f.g: Son of Herod the Great, ruler of Judea from 4 BC to AD 6.
The northern region of Israel.

chapters.n: They settled in Nazareth, a small, unimportant village. Matthew says this fulfilled “He shall be called a Nazarene” — perhaps a wordplay on the Hebrew netzer, “branch,” a messianic title.

f.g: Possibly linked to netzer (“Branch”) in Isaiah 11:1.

chapters.n: About thirty years later, John the Baptist appears preaching in the Judean desert near the Jordan River. He was Jesus’s relative, born six months before Him.

f.g: Decades after chapter 2; JST adds details of Jesus growing up and waiting upon the Lord.
The dry hill country east of Jerusalem, sloping to the Jordan and Dead Sea.

chapters.n: His message: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near!” To repent means to turn — change your mind, heart, and direction.

f.g: Greek metanoeō — to change one’s mind and turn around.
Matthew’s usual phrase for the kingdom of God; Jews often avoided saying God’s name directly.

chapters.n: John is the voice Isaiah foretold, crying in the wilderness to prepare the Lord’s way and make His paths straight.

f.g: Isaiah.

f.w: The voice of one crying in the wilderness

chapters.n: John wore camel-hair clothing with a leather belt and ate locusts and wild honey — simple desert food. His dress resembled the prophet Elijah’s.

f.g: Grasshoppers, permitted as food under the law (Leviticus 11:22).
Food.

chapters.n: Crowds came from Jerusalem, all Judea, and the Jordan region.

f.g: The river running from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: They were baptized by John in the Jordan, openly confessing their sins.

f.g: Greek baptizō — to immerse.

chapters.n: When Pharisees and Sadducees came, John called them a brood of snakes: “Who warned you to flee coming judgment?” He sees through religious show.

f.g: A strict Jewish party devoted to detailed obedience to the law and oral traditions.
A priestly, aristocratic party that rejected the resurrection and oral law.
Offspring of poisonous snakes.

chapters.n: Show real repentance by the way you live — produce fruit that matches it.

f.g: Fruit fitting, worthy of repentance.

chapters.n: Don’t rely on being Abraham’s descendants; God could make children of Abraham from these stones. Covenant blessings depend on faithfulness, not ancestry.

f.w: We have Abraham to our father

f.g: In Aramaic/Hebrew a likely pun: “stones” (abanim) and “sons” (banim).

chapters.n: The axe is already at the root of the trees; every unfruitful tree will be cut down and burned. Judgment is near.

f.w: the axe is laid unto the root of the trees
every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit

chapters.n: John baptizes with water for repentance, but One more powerful is coming — whose sandals John isn’t worthy to carry. He will baptize with the Holy Ghost and fire.

f.w: whose shoes I am not worthy to bear
f.g: Carrying sandals was a servant’s lowliest task.

f.w: with the Holy Ghost, and with fire

chapters.n: Like a farmer with a winnowing fork, He will clear His threshing floor, store the wheat in the barn, and burn the chaff. He will separate the faithful from the unfaithful.

f.g: A winnowing fork, used to toss grain so the wind blows away the chaff.
Granary, barn.

chapters.n: Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.
John objects: “I need to be baptized by You, and You come to me?” He recognizes Jesus’s greater holiness.

f.g: Tried to prevent.

chapters.n: Jesus answers: “Let it be so now; it is right for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Though sinless, Jesus was baptized to obey the Father and show the way. Nephi explains this beautifully.

f.w: Suffer it to be so now
f.g: Permit it, allow it.

chapters.n: Coming up out of the water — showing baptism by immersion — Jesus saw the heavens open and the Spirit of God descend like a dove upon Him.

f.w: went up straightway out of the water

chapters.n: The Father’s voice declares, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” All three members of the Godhead are present and distinct: the Son baptized, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking.
Right after His baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness. The Joseph Smith Translation says He went “to be with God,” and the temptations came afterward.

f.w: led up of the Spirit into the wilderness
f.g: JST: “led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be with God.”

chapters.n: Jesus fasted forty days and nights and afterward was hungry. Moses and Elijah also fasted forty days; Israel wandered forty years. Jesus succeeds where Israel struggled.

f.g: Hungry. JST adds that He had been communing with God.

chapters.n: The tempter comes: “If you are the Son of God, turn these stones into bread.” Satan targets physical hunger and tries to make Jesus doubt the Father’s declaration at His baptism.

f.w: If thou be the Son of God

chapters.n: Jesus answers with scripture: people need more than bread — they live by every word from God. He uses God’s word as His defense.

f.w: Man shall not live by bread alone

chapters.n: Next, Jesus is taken to Jerusalem and stands on the high corner of the temple. JST says the Spirit set Him there, not the devil.

f.g: Jerusalem.
The highest point or wing of the temple complex, high above the Kidron Valley.
JST: “Jesus was in the holy city, and the Spirit setteth him on the pinnacle of the temple.”

chapters.n: Satan now quotes scripture himself: “Throw Yourself down — God promised angels would catch You.” Scripture can be twisted out of context to justify wrong.

f.w: He shall give his angels charge concerning thee

chapters.n: Jesus replies, “It is also written: Don’t put the Lord your God to the test.” Faith trusts God; it doesn’t demand that He prove Himself.

f.w: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God

chapters.n: Finally Jesus is shown all the kingdoms of the world and their splendor from a very high mountain.

f.g: JST again says the Spirit, not the devil, took Him there.

f.w: all the kingdoms of the world

chapters.n: Satan offers it all — if Jesus will bow and worship him. The temptation is to gain power by a shortcut that bypasses the cross.
Jesus commands, “Get away, Satan!” and cites scripture: worship and serve God alone. Moses rebuked Satan in a similar way.

f.w: Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God

chapters.n: The devil leaves, and angels come and minister to Jesus. Resisting temptation brings heavenly help.

f.w: angels came and ministered unto him

chapters.n: When Jesus hears John has been imprisoned, He goes to Galilee to begin His public ministry there.
He moves from Nazareth to Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee in the old tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. Capernaum became His ministry base.

f.g: A town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.
Zebulun and Naphtali, two of Israel’s tribes.

chapters.n: This fulfilled a prophecy of Isaiah.

f.g: Isaiah.

chapters.n: Isaiah named this region — Zebulun, Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles. It was the first area conquered by Assyria and later heavily mixed with Gentiles, yet it would see the Messiah first.
People sitting in darkness have seen a great light. Jesus is that light, dawning on those overshadowed by death.

f.w: The people which sat in darkness saw great light

f.g: Deep darkness.

chapters.n: From then on Jesus preached, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” — the same message as John.

f.w: Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand

chapters.n: Walking along the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon (Peter) and Andrew, casting nets — fishermen at work.

f.g: Peter (Greek Petros) means “rock”; Jesus gave him this name.
A freshwater lake about 13 miles (21 km) long, also called Gennesaret or Tiberias.

chapters.n: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” Jesus turns their skills to a new purpose: gathering people to God.
They left their nets immediately and followed Him. Their quick response is a model of discipleship.

f.g: Immediately.

chapters.n: A little farther on, Jesus calls two more brothers, James and John, who were mending nets in a boat with their father Zebedee.

f.w: James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother

f.g: Repairing, preparing.

chapters.n: They also left at once — the boat and even their father — to follow Jesus. Discipleship can require leaving what is familiar.

f.w: left the ship and their father

chapters.n: Jesus traveled throughout Galilee, teaching in synagogues, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease. Teaching, preaching, and healing summarize His ministry.

f.g: Local Jewish meeting houses for scripture reading, prayer, and teaching.
Good news.

chapters.n: His fame spread throughout the Roman province of Syria. People brought the sick, suffering, demon-possessed, those with seizures, and paralyzed — and He healed them all.

f.g: Various.
Probably those suffering seizures (epilepsy).
Paralysis.

chapters.n: Huge crowds followed Him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan — from every direction.

f.g: “Ten Cities” — a league of mostly Gentile Greek cities east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up a mountainside and sits down — the usual posture of a Jewish teacher. His disciples gather close. Like Moses giving the law on a mountain, Jesus gives His higher law. The resurrected Savior gave a similar sermon at the temple in Bountiful (3 Nephi 12–14).

f.w: he went up into a mountain

f.g: When He sat down — teachers sat to teach.

chapters.n: Jesus begins teaching. Chapters 5–7 are called the Sermon on the Mount.

f.g: A formal way of introducing a solemn teaching.

chapters.n: The first of the Beatitudes (“blessings”). Those who recognize their spiritual need are truly blessed — the kingdom is theirs. In 3 Nephi the Savior adds “who come unto me.”

f.g: Greek makarios — truly happy, favored by God.

chapters.n: Those who mourn — for sin, loss, or the world’s suffering — will be comforted by God.
The meek — gentle, humble, teachable — will inherit the earth, quoting Psalm 37. Meekness is strength under control, not weakness.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. The Book of Mormon version adds “with the Holy Ghost.”
The merciful will receive mercy. How we treat others shapes how we will be treated.
The pure in heart — sincere, single-minded, clean — will see God. A promise Latter-day Saints take literally.
Peacemakers — those who actively make peace — will be called God’s children, because they act like Him.
Those persecuted for doing right are blessed; the kingdom of heaven is theirs.
Jesus applies it personally: you are blessed when people insult, persecute, and lie about you because of Me.

f.g: Insult, abuse verbally.

chapters.n: Rejoice and be glad, for your reward in heaven is great — they persecuted the prophets the same way. Joseph Smith received similar comfort.
You are the salt of the earth — preserving and adding flavor. But salt that loses its saltiness is useless. Disciples must stay true to be useful.

f.g: Flavor, taste.

chapters.n: You are the light of the world, like a city on a hill that can’t be hidden.

f.w: Ye are the light of the world

chapters.n: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a basket; they put it on a stand to light the whole house.

f.g: A small oil lamp.
A basket or measuring container.
Lampstand.

chapters.n: Let your light shine so others see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven. The goal is to point people to God, not ourselves.
Jesus hasn’t come to abolish the law of Moses or the prophets, but to fulfill them — to bring them to their full purpose in Himself.

f.w: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil

chapters.n: Not even the smallest letter or stroke of the law will pass away until everything is fulfilled.

f.g: The Greek iota, the smallest letter — like the Hebrew yod.
A tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.

chapters.n: Whoever breaks even a small commandment and teaches others to, will be least in the kingdom; whoever keeps and teaches them will be great. Teachers carry extra responsibility.
Your righteousness must go beyond the scribes’ and Pharisees’ — beyond outward rule-keeping to a changed heart. In 3 Nephi, the Savior says instead “except ye shall keep my commandments.”

f.w: exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees

chapters.n: Now six contrasts: “You have heard… but I say.” The first: the old law says, “Don’t murder.”

f.g: The local court.

chapters.n: Jesus goes to the root: anger and contempt. Calling someone “Raca” (empty-head) or “fool” shows a heart that could lead to murder. The Book of Mormon and JST omit “without a cause,” making the standard even higher.

f.g: Absent from 3 Nephi 12:22 and the JST.
An Aramaic insult meaning “empty-headed.”
The Sanhedrin, the high Jewish court.
Literally “the Gehenna of fire” — named after a valley outside Jerusalem where trash burned.

chapters.n: So if you are offering a gift at the altar and remember someone has something against you —

f.g: An offering at the temple.
Anything.

chapters.n: — leave your gift, go make things right, then come back and offer it. Reconciliation with others comes before worship. In 3 Nephi: “come unto me with full purpose of heart.”

f.w: first be reconciled to thy brother

chapters.n: Settle disputes quickly while you can, before they end up in court and you go to prison.
You won’t get out until you pay the last penny. Unresolved wrongs carry a cost.

f.g: A tiny Roman coin; 3 Nephi 12:26 uses the Nephite “senine.”

chapters.n: Second contrast: the law says, “Don’t commit adultery.”
Jesus says lustful looking is already adultery in the heart. Purity begins with thoughts.

f.w: looketh on a woman to lust after her

chapters.n: If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out — better to lose one part than your whole self. This is hyperbole: deal decisively with whatever leads to sin.

f.g: Cause to stumble, lead into sin.
JST and 3 Nephi 12:29-30 explain it as not allowing these things to enter the heart; taking up one’s cross.

chapters.n: If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. Remove what tempts you, even if it’s painful.

f.w: if thy right hand offend thee

chapters.n: Third contrast: the law allowed divorce with a written certificate.
Jesus raises the standard: divorce except for unfaithfulness leads to adultery. He restores God’s original intent for lasting marriage.

f.w: saving for the cause of fornication

f.g: Divorce.

chapters.n: Fourth contrast: the law said don’t break your oaths; keep your vows to the Lord.

f.g: Swear falsely; break an oath.

f.w: perform unto the Lord thine oaths

chapters.n: Jesus says don’t swear oaths at all — not by heaven, which is God’s throne.
Nor by the earth (His footstool) or Jerusalem (the great King’s city). People tried to make “lesser” oaths they could break; Jesus says everything belongs to God.

f.w: the city of the great King

chapters.n: Don’t even swear by your own head — you can’t make one hair white or black. We don’t control even ourselves.

f.w: thou canst not make one hair white or black
f.g: A reminder of how little we control.

chapters.n: Simply let your “yes” mean yes and your “no” mean no. Honesty shouldn’t need oaths.

f.g: Speech, words.
Or “from the evil one.”

chapters.n: Fifth contrast: the law of “an eye for an eye” limited revenge to fair punishment by courts.
Jesus says don’t retaliate. If someone slaps your right cheek — an insulting backhand — turn the other also. Respond to insult without revenge.

f.g: Don’t retaliate against an evil person.

f.w: turn to him the other also

chapters.n: If someone sues for your shirt, let them have your coat too — go beyond what’s demanded.

f.g: The inner tunic.
The outer robe, which the law said could not be kept overnight (Exodus 22:26-27).

chapters.n: If forced to carry something a mile — as Roman soldiers could require — go two. Turn compulsion into service.

f.w: compel thee to go a mile
f.g: Roman soldiers could legally force civilians to carry gear one mile.
Two.

chapters.n: Give to those who ask, and don’t turn away those who want to borrow. Generosity reflects God’s own giving.

f.w: Give to him that asketh thee

chapters.n: Sixth contrast: “Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” The law commanded love of neighbor; “hate your enemy” was a popular addition.
Jesus commands: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you. This is the heart of Christlike love.

f.g: Mistreat, insult.

chapters.n: Then you will be true children of your Father, who sends sun and rain on good and bad alike. Loving enemies makes us like God.

f.w: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good

chapters.n: If you love only those who love you, what reward is that? Even tax collectors do that.

f.g: Tax collectors for Rome, despised as collaborators and cheats.

chapters.n: If you greet only your own people, what are you doing beyond others? Disciples are called to more.

f.g: Greet warmly.

chapters.n: “Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” The Greek suggests complete, whole, mature. After His resurrection Jesus said “even as I, or your Father” (3 Nephi 12:48). Perfection is a lifelong goal reached through Christ’s grace.

f.g: Greek teleios — complete, whole, fully developed.

chapters.n: Be careful not to do your good deeds just to be seen by others; then there’s no reward from God. Jesus now addresses motives in three acts of devotion: giving, praying, and fasting.

f.g: Gifts to the poor; also good deeds generally (some manuscripts say “righteousness”).

chapters.n: When you give, don’t trumpet it like the hypocrites in synagogues and streets who want praise. They already have their reward — people’s applause, nothing more.

f.g: Greek hypokritēs — a stage actor wearing a mask.
Paid in full — the attention they wanted is all they get.

chapters.n: When you give, don’t let your left hand know what your right is doing — keep it quiet, even from yourself, avoiding self-congratulation.

f.w: let not thy left hand know
f.g: A picture of giving so naturally that you don’t keep score.

chapters.n: Give in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

f.w: thy Father which seeth in secret

chapters.n: When you pray, don’t be like hypocrites who love to pray on street corners to be seen.

f.g: Standing was a normal posture for prayer.

f.w: that they may be seen of men

chapters.n: Instead, go into your private room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. He will reward you. Private prayer builds a real relationship with God.

f.g: An inner room or storeroom — a private space.

chapters.n: Don’t babble on with empty, repeated phrases like the pagans, who think they’ll be heard for using many words.

f.g: Meaningless babbling; mechanical, thoughtless words.

chapters.n: Your Father already knows what you need before you ask. Prayer isn’t informing God; it aligns our will with His.

f.w: your Father knoweth what things ye have need of

chapters.n: Jesus gives a pattern for prayer, not a script to repeat mechanically. It begins by addressing God as our Father in heaven and honoring His name as holy.

f.g: In this way — a model, not a formula.
Treated as holy, honored.

f.w: Our Father which art in heaven

chapters.n: Pray for God’s kingdom to come and His will to be done on earth as in heaven. Our wishes yield to His. (The Nephite version of the prayer omits “Thy kingdom come.”)
Ask for what we need today — one day at a time — trusting God as Israel trusted for manna.

f.g: The Greek word may mean “bread for today” or “for tomorrow.” This line is omitted in 3 Nephi 13.

chapters.n: Ask forgiveness for our debts (sins) as we forgive those who owe us. Sin is pictured as a debt we can’t pay.

f.g: Sins, moral debts; Luke 11:4 uses “sins.”

chapters.n: Ask God to keep us from temptation and rescue us from evil. The closing praise of His kingdom, power, and glory forever is absent in some early manuscripts but appears in 3 Nephi 13:13.

f.g: JST: “And suffer us not to be led into temptation.”

chapters.n: Jesus explains one line: if you forgive others, your Father will forgive you.

f.g: Wrongs, offenses.

f.w: if ye forgive men their trespasses

chapters.n: But if you refuse to forgive, God won’t forgive you. Forgiving others opens our own hearts to receive forgiveness.

f.w: if ye forgive not men their trespasses

chapters.n: When you fast, don’t look gloomy like the hypocrites, who make their faces miserable so others notice. That’s all the reward they get.

f.g: Leave faces unwashed, put on ashes — making a show of fasting.

chapters.n: When you fast, groom yourself normally — oil your hair and wash your face.

f.g: Put oil on your hair — normal daily grooming, a sign of gladness.

chapters.n: Then no one but your Father will know you’re fasting, and He will reward you. Fasting is between us and God.

f.w: thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly

chapters.n: Don’t store up treasures on earth, where moths eat clothes, rust (or decay) destroys, and thieves break in. Earthly wealth is fragile.

f.g: Corrosion or decay of any kind.
Literally “dig through” — mud-brick walls.

chapters.n: Store up treasures in heaven instead, where nothing can destroy or steal them.
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. What we value most directs our affections.
The eye is the body’s lamp. If your eye is “single” — focused, generous, clear — your whole life is full of light.

f.g: Healthy, undivided, sincere; also suggests generosity.

f.w: if therefore thine eye be single

chapters.n: But if your eye is “evil” — greedy, envious — your whole life is dark. And if your inner light has become darkness, how deep that darkness is!

f.g: Diseased; in Jewish idiom, an “evil eye” meant greed or stinginess.

chapters.n: No one can serve two masters. You can’t serve both God and money. Ultimately we choose who rules us.

f.g: Aramaic for wealth or possessions, here personified as a rival god.

f.w: No man can serve two masters

chapters.n: So don’t be anxious about food, drink, or clothing. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothes? In 3 Nephi, Jesus directed this especially to the Twelve He called to full-time ministry.

f.g: Don’t be anxious or worry (old English “thought” meant anxiety).

f.w: Take no thought for your life

chapters.n: Look at the birds: they don’t plant, harvest, or store, yet your Father feeds them. You are worth far more.

f.g: Birds.

chapters.n: Can worrying add a single hour to your life? Worry accomplishes nothing.

f.w: add one cubit unto his stature
f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches; the phrase may mean adding height or a little time to one’s life.

chapters.n: Why worry about clothes? Look how wildflowers grow — they don’t work or spin thread.

f.g: Wildflowers, perhaps anemones or poppies that carpet Galilee in spring.
Make thread for weaving cloth.

chapters.n: Yet not even King Solomon in all his splendor was dressed as beautifully as one of them.
If God dresses short-lived wild grass so beautifully, won’t He much more care for you, you of little faith?

f.g: Dried grass was used as fuel.

chapters.n: So don’t worry, saying, “What will we eat, drink, or wear?”

f.g: With what.

chapters.n: Those without faith chase after all these things, but your Father knows you need them.

f.g: Here, those who don’t know God.

chapters.n: Seek first God’s kingdom and His righteousness, and everything else will be provided. The JST reads “seek ye first to build up the kingdom of God.” Priorities matter.

f.w: seek ye first the kingdom of God

chapters.n: Don’t worry about tomorrow; it will bring its own concerns. Each day has enough trouble of its own. Live faithfully one day at a time.

f.w: Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof
f.g: Each day has enough trouble; don’t borrow tomorrow’s.

chapters.n: Jesus warns against condemning others. He isn’t forbidding all judgment of right and wrong, but the harsh, self-righteous kind that writes people off.

f.g: The JST reads “Judge not unrighteously, that ye be not judged: but judge righteous judgment.”

chapters.n: The standard we use on others is the standard God will use on us. Merciful people receive mercy; harsh people invite harshness.

f.g: mete = measure out, as grain is measured in a container.

chapters.n: A deliberately funny picture: a man with a whole wooden beam stuck in his eye fussing over a speck of sawdust in someone else’s. We see others’ small faults while missing our own large ones.

f.g: mote = a tiny speck or splinter.
A large timber, like a roof rafter — intentional exaggeration.

chapters.n: Jesus presses the image further: how absurd to offer help with someone else’s speck while a beam blocks your own sight.

f.w: Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye

chapters.n: The fix is to deal honestly with our own sins first. Then, humbled and seeing clearly, we can actually help others instead of just criticizing them.

f.g: Greek hypokritēs — originally a stage actor wearing a mask; someone playing a part.

chapters.n: Sacred things should be shared with wisdom. Dogs and pigs (unclean animals to Jews) picture people who would mock or trample what is holy rather than receive it.

f.g: The JST adds that the mysteries of the kingdom are to be kept within oneself and not shared with the world.

chapters.n: A warm invitation to pray. The three verbs grow in effort — ask, seek, knock — and each comes with a promise that God will respond.

f.w: Ask, and it shall be given you

chapters.n: The promise is for “every one,” not just the important or righteous few. God hears every sincere seeker.
Jesus appeals to common sense: what parent would hand a hungry child a stone that looks like a loaf of bread?

f.g: Round flat loaves in Galilee could resemble stones, sharpening the contrast.

chapters.n: Or give a snake that looks a bit like a fish? No loving parent tricks a child like that.
The point lands here: if imperfect earthly parents give good gifts, our perfect Heavenly Father will be even more generous to those who ask.

f.g: Compared with God’s perfect goodness, all mortals fall short.

chapters.n: The “Golden Rule.” Treat others the way you want to be treated — Jesus says this sums up the whole message of the Old Testament.

f.g: A common name for the Hebrew scriptures as a whole.

chapters.n: There are two ways through life. The easy, popular road leads to ruin; it takes no effort to drift onto it.

f.g: strait = narrow, tight (not “straight”).

chapters.n: The road to eternal life is narrow and demanding, and fewer people choose it — but it leads where we truly want to go.
Jesus warns of false teachers who look harmless and religious on the outside but are dangerous and greedy within.

f.g: ravening = ravenous, greedy for prey.

chapters.n: The test of any teacher is the fruit of their life and teaching. Thornbushes never produce grapes; bad sources don’t produce truly good results.
Character shows itself over time. A healthy tree naturally bears good fruit; a rotten one bears bad fruit.

f.g: Greek sapros — rotten, decayed, worthless.

chapters.n: Jesus restates the principle firmly: what we really are inside eventually comes out in what we produce.

f.w: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit

chapters.n: Fruitless trees are cut down and burned — a sober image of final judgment, echoing John the Baptist’s preaching.

f.w: hewn down, and cast into the fire

chapters.n: Jesus closes the thought by repeating the key line: watch the fruit, and you will know the tree.

f.w: by their fruits ye shall know them

chapters.n: Calling Jesus “Lord” isn’t enough. Entrance into God’s kingdom comes to those who actually do the Father’s will.

f.w: doeth the will of my Father

chapters.n: At the judgment some will point to impressive religious works done in Christ’s name. Outward displays don’t substitute for a changed heart.

f.g: The day of judgment.

chapters.n: The heart of the matter is relationship. Those who never truly came to know Christ — though busy in his name — will hear, “I never knew you.”

f.g: The JST reads “Ye never knew me,” placing the failure on the hearers.

chapters.n: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with a parable. Hearing and then doing his words is like building a house on solid rock.
Storms come to everyone — rain, floods, wind. The house on the rock still stands because of what it’s founded on.

f.g: In Palestine, dry streambeds (wadis) could suddenly become torrents after heavy rain.

chapters.n: Hearing without doing is like building on sand. Everything may look fine until the storm comes.
The same storm hits, and this house collapses completely. The difference between the two builders was never the weather, but the foundation.

f.w: great was the fall of it

chapters.n: The crowd was amazed. Matthew marks the end of the sermon with a formula he uses after each of Jesus’s major discourses.

f.w: when Jesus had ended these sayings

f.g: doctrine = teaching.

chapters.n: Scribes taught by quoting earlier rabbis. Jesus spoke on his own authority — “I say unto you” — as the one who gave the law in the first place.

f.g: Professional experts who copied and interpreted the law of Moses.

chapters.n: After the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew turns from Jesus’s words to his works. Chapters 8–9 gather a series of miracles showing his power over disease, nature, evil, and death.
A leper kneels before Jesus. He doesn’t doubt Jesus’s power — only whether Jesus is willing to help someone like him.

f.g: Leprosy in the Bible covered various skin diseases; sufferers were ritually unclean and lived apart from society.
if thou wilt = if you are willing.

chapters.n: Jesus touches the untouchable. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean, but here Jesus’s touch makes the leper clean instead.
Jesus sends the man to the priest to follow the law of Moses for cleansed lepers. Being officially declared clean would restore him to his family and community.

f.g: Jesus often discouraged publicity, perhaps to avoid crowds seeking only signs or stirring political hopes.

chapters.n: In Capernaum, Jesus’s home base in Galilee, a Roman army officer comes to him for help — a Gentile reaching out to a Jewish teacher.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about 100 soldiers.

chapters.n: The centurion’s servant is paralyzed and suffering badly. That a powerful officer cares so much for a servant says something about his character.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

chapters.n: Jesus immediately offers to go to the Gentile’s house — something many Jews would have avoided to stay ritually clean.

f.w: I will come and heal him

chapters.n: The centurion humbly says he isn’t worthy to host Jesus. He believes Jesus’s word alone is enough to heal, even from a distance.
As a soldier he understands authority: orders given are orders carried out. He recognizes that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness.

f.w: I am a man under authority
f.g: He serves under higher command and also commands others — so he knows how authority works.

chapters.n: Jesus is amazed. This outsider shows more faith than he has found among his own covenant people.
Jesus foresees people from every nation joining the patriarchs at God’s great feast. Faith, not ancestry, opens the kingdom.

f.g: Literally “recline,” as guests did at a banquet table.

chapters.n: Those who assumed they belonged by birth may be shut out if they reject him. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” describes the bitter regret of the lost.

f.g: Those who by lineage were heirs to the covenant — here, Israelites who reject the Messiah.
Grinding the teeth in anguish or anger.

chapters.n: Jesus grants the request exactly as the centurion believed, and the servant is healed at that very moment, without Jesus ever entering the house.

f.g: selfsame = the very same.

chapters.n: At Peter’s home in Capernaum, Jesus finds Peter’s mother-in-law in bed with a fever. This quiet detail also shows Peter was married.
A simple touch heals her completely — no lingering weakness — and she rises at once to serve. Healing leads naturally to service.

f.g: ministered = served, likely by preparing food and caring for guests.

chapters.n: As evening falls, crowds bring the sick and the possessed. Jesus heals them all by his word.

f.g: even = evening. Mark notes it was the sabbath, which ended at sunset.

chapters.n: Matthew sees these healings as fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy about the suffering Servant who would carry our burdens — physical as well as spiritual.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah (Greek form of the name).

chapters.n: Seeing the crowds, Jesus decides to cross the Sea of Galilee to the eastern shore.

f.g: The eastern, largely Gentile shore of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: A scribe eagerly promises to follow Jesus anywhere. Jesus will test whether he has counted the cost.

f.g: An expert in the law of Moses; most scribes opposed Jesus, making this offer unusual.
whithersoever = wherever.

chapters.n: Jesus warns that following him means giving up comfort and security. Even animals have homes, but he has none.

f.g: Jesus’s favorite title for himself, echoing Daniel 7:13; in LDS teaching it also points to him as Son of the Man of Holiness, God the Father.

chapters.n: Another disciple asks to wait until he has buried his father — possibly meaning until his father dies, which could be years away.

f.g: suffer = allow, permit.

chapters.n: Jesus’s startling reply puts discipleship first: let the spiritually dead take care of such matters; the call to follow can’t wait.

f.w: let the dead bury their dead
f.g: Likely meaning: let those who are spiritually dead bury the physically dead.

chapters.n: Jesus gets into a boat, and his disciples follow — they are literally “following” him into what will become a test of faith.

f.g: A fishing boat; one from this era was found in the Sea of Galilee in 1986, about 27 feet long.

chapters.n: A sudden violent storm swamps the boat, yet Jesus sleeps. The Sea of Galilee lies low among hills, and fierce winds can drop onto it without warning.

f.g: Greek seismos — literally a “shaking,” the word often used for earthquakes.

chapters.n: Terrified, the disciples wake him with a short, desperate prayer: “Lord, save us: we perish.”
Jesus first calms the disciples’ fear, then the sea. With a word he rebukes wind and waves, and everything goes still.

f.w: rebuked the winds and the sea

chapters.n: The disciples ask the right question. In the Old Testament only God rules the sea — so who is this man?

f.w: What manner of man is this

chapters.n: On the eastern shore two violently possessed men live among the tombs, terrorizing the area. Mark and Luke focus on one of them.

f.g: Other manuscripts read Gadarenes or Gerasenes — towns in the region east of the sea.
Tombs were unclean places; living there marked these men as outcasts.

chapters.n: The evil spirits recognize Jesus as the Son of God before most people do, and they fear the judgment they know is coming.

f.g: Before the appointed day of final judgment.

f.w: What have we to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “Why are you bothering us?”

chapters.n: A large herd of pigs is feeding nearby — a sign this was a Gentile area, since Jews didn’t raise unclean animals.
The spirits beg to enter the pigs. Latter-day Saint teaching notes that spirits without bodies crave one — even an animal’s.

f.g: besought = begged.

chapters.n: With one word, “Go,” Jesus frees the men. The herd stampedes into the sea — showing how destructive these spirits were.

f.g: A steep slope or cliff above the lake.

chapters.n: The herdsmen run to town and report everything, both the lost pigs and the healed men.

f.g: The herdsmen.

chapters.n: Rather than rejoice, the townspeople ask Jesus to leave. Perhaps their financial loss or fear of his power mattered more to them than two restored lives.

f.g: coasts = borders, region (not seashore).

chapters.n: Turned away by the Gergesenes, Jesus sails back across the Sea of Galilee to Capernaum, which Matthew calls “his own city” because Jesus made his home there.
Friends carry a paralyzed man to Jesus. Seeing their faith, Jesus speaks first to the man’s deepest need: forgiveness of sins.
Some scribes silently accuse Jesus of blasphemy, reasoning that only God can forgive sins. They are right about God — and wrong about Jesus.

f.g: blaspheme = speak irreverently of God or claim what belongs only to God.

chapters.n: Jesus reads their thoughts — itself a sign of who he is — and challenges their hidden accusation.

f.g: wherefore = why.

chapters.n: Anyone can claim to forgive sins, since no one can see it happen. Telling a paralyzed man to walk is easily tested.

f.g: whether = which of the two.

chapters.n: So Jesus does the visible miracle to prove the invisible one: the healing shows he truly has power to forgive sins.

f.w: power on earth to forgive sins

chapters.n: The man stands, picks up his mat, and walks home — living proof of Jesus’s authority.
The crowds respond with awe and praise God for giving such power to a man.
Jesus calls Matthew, a tax collector, from his tax booth. Matthew, the traditional author of this Gospel, leaves everything immediately.

f.g: The tax office or toll booth where duties were collected.
Also called Levi in Mark and Luke.

chapters.n: At a meal in Matthew’s house, many tax collectors and “sinners” eat with Jesus. Sharing a meal signaled acceptance and friendship.

f.g: Tax collectors who worked for Rome; Jews often viewed them as traitors and cheats.
sat at meat = reclined at a meal.

chapters.n: The Pharisees, who carefully avoided contact with sinners to stay ritually pure, are scandalized that Jesus would eat with such people.

f.g: A strict, influential Jewish group devoted to exact observance of the law and oral traditions.

chapters.n: Jesus answers with a proverb: doctors go where the sick are. He came for those who know they need healing.
Quoting Hosea, Jesus says God values mercy more than ritual. Ironically, those who think themselves righteous may not hear his call.

f.w: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice
not come to call the righteous

chapters.n: Disciples of John the Baptist ask why Jesus’s disciples don’t fast as they and the Pharisees regularly do.

f.g: Many Pharisees fasted twice a week.

chapters.n: Wedding guests don’t mourn while the groom is with them. Jesus is the Bridegroom; fasting will fit after he is taken away — a hint of his death.

f.g: The groom’s friends and wedding guests.

chapters.n: You don’t patch old cloth with unshrunk new fabric — it will pull away and tear worse. Jesus’s gospel isn’t just a patch on old traditions.

f.g: rent = tear.
Unshrunk cloth that would shrink when washed.

chapters.n: New wine expands as it ferments and would burst old, stiff leather wineskins. The new covenant needs new “containers” — renewed hearts and forms.

f.g: bottles = wineskins made of animal hide.

chapters.n: A synagogue ruler named Jairus (named in Mark and Luke) comes to Jesus. His daughter has just died, yet he believes Jesus can restore her.

f.g: A leader who oversaw synagogue services.

chapters.n: Jesus rises at once and goes with the grieving father, his disciples following.
On the way, a woman who has bled for twelve years — making her ritually unclean and isolated — reaches out and touches the edge of his clothing.

f.g: Continual bleeding, probably a menstrual disorder.
Likely the tassel (tzitzit) that observant Jewish men wore on their cloak corners.

chapters.n: She believes even a touch will heal her. Her faith is quiet and private, but very real.

f.g: whole = healed; the Greek word also means saved.

chapters.n: Jesus turns, calls her “Daughter,” and credits her faith. She is healed physically and publicly welcomed back.

f.w: thy faith hath made thee whole

chapters.n: At the ruler’s house, funeral mourners are already wailing and playing flutes, as was customary even for poor families.

f.g: Flute players hired for funeral mourning.

chapters.n: Jesus says the girl is only sleeping — death is not final in his presence. The mourners mock him, knowing she is dead.

f.g: Mocked him with ridicule.

chapters.n: Sending out the scoffers, Jesus takes her by the hand and she rises. It foreshadows his power over death itself.
News of the miracle spreads throughout the region.

f.g: The report of this event.

chapters.n: Two blind men follow Jesus, calling him “Son of David” — a messianic title. They recognize who he is even though they can’t see him.
Indoors, Jesus asks whether they believe he can heal them. Their simple answer: “Yea, Lord.”

f.w: Believe ye that I am able to do this?

chapters.n: Jesus touches their eyes and heals them according to their faith — a pattern repeated throughout these chapters.
Their sight returns. Jesus sternly tells them to keep quiet about it.

f.g: straitly = strictly, sternly.

chapters.n: Overjoyed, they tell everyone anyway, spreading his fame further.
As the healed men leave, people bring a man who cannot speak because of an evil spirit.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak.

chapters.n: When the spirit is cast out, the man speaks. The amazed crowds say nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.

f.w: It was never so seen in Israel

chapters.n: The Pharisees can’t deny the miracle, so they attribute it to Satan. This accusation will return and be answered in chapter 12.
A summary of Jesus’s ministry: teaching, preaching, and healing in every town — almost word for word the same summary as 4:23, framing the section.
Jesus feels deep compassion for the crowds. They are exhausted and lost, like sheep with no shepherd to guide or protect them.

f.g: Greek splanchnizomai — a deep, gut-level feeling of pity.

chapters.n: He changes the image to a harvest: many people are ready to receive the gospel, but there are too few workers to gather them.
His answer is to pray for more laborers — and in the next chapter he sends out his own Twelve as answers to that prayer.
Jesus gives his twelve disciples the same power he has been using — over evil spirits and every disease. Authority to act for him is formally given, not assumed.
Matthew lists the Twelve Apostles in pairs. Peter always comes first in these lists, reflecting his role as their leader.

f.g: Greek apostolos — “one who is sent,” an authorized messenger.

f.w: The first, Simon, who is called Peter

chapters.n: The list continues. Matthew humbly identifies himself as “the publican,” remembering the despised job he left to follow Jesus.

f.g: Probably the same apostle Luke calls Judas the brother (or son) of James.
Often identified with Nathanael.

chapters.n: The list ends with a sobering note: Judas Iscariot, “who also betrayed him.” Even among the chosen, agency remains.

f.g: From Aramaic qan’an, “zealous” — Luke calls him Simon Zelotes.
Possibly “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea.

chapters.n: For this first mission, Jesus tells the Twelve not to go to Gentiles or Samaritans. The gospel would go first to Israel and later to all the world.

f.w: Go not into the way of the Gentiles

f.g: A people of mixed Israelite descent living between Judea and Galilee, long at odds with the Jews.

chapters.n: Israel is pictured as a flock of lost sheep needing shepherds — tying back to Jesus’s compassion in 9:36.

f.w: lost sheep of the house of Israel

chapters.n: Their message is the same one John the Baptist and Jesus preached: God’s kingdom has come near.

f.w: The kingdom of heaven is at hand

chapters.n: The apostles are to do what Jesus has done — heal, cleanse, raise, and cast out — and never charge for it. Gifts freely received should be freely shared.

f.w: freely ye have received, freely give

chapters.n: They are to take no money. Traveling without funds would teach them to rely on God and on the people they served.

f.g: Literally belts or girdles, where coins were often carried.
brass = copper coins, the lowest value.

chapters.n: No travel bag, spare clothing, or extra gear. Those who labor in God’s work deserve to be supported by those they serve.

f.g: scrip = a traveler’s bag for food.

f.w: the workman is worthy of his meat

chapters.n: In each town they should find a worthy host and stay with that family rather than moving from house to house.

f.w: there abide till ye go thence
f.g: Stay there until you leave that place.

chapters.n: On entering a home they should greet it — usually with the Hebrew blessing “Peace be to this house.”

f.g: salute = greet.

chapters.n: If the household welcomes them, their blessing of peace rests there; if not, the blessing comes back to them — nothing is lost.

f.w: let your peace return to you

chapters.n: Shaking dust off the feet was a symbolic act showing that the messengers had done their duty and the responsibility now rested on those who refused.

f.w: shake off the dust of your feet

chapters.n: Rejecting Christ’s authorized servants is serious. Sodom and Gomorrah never had such an opportunity, so their judgment will be lighter.

f.g: more bearable.

chapters.n: Jesus is honest about danger. His messengers need to be shrewd like serpents yet innocent like doves — wise without becoming harmful.

f.w: wise as serpents, and harmless as doves

f.g: Greek akeraios — pure, unmixed, without guile.

chapters.n: Persecution is coming. Local Jewish councils will try them, and they will be whipped in synagogues.

f.g: Local Jewish courts (sanhedrins).
scourge = whip.

chapters.n: They will even stand before Gentile rulers — and these trials will become opportunities to bear witness of Christ.
When on trial they shouldn’t panic about what to say; the words they need will be given in the moment.

f.g: take no thought = don’t be anxious.

chapters.n: The Holy Spirit himself will speak through them. This is a promise of divine help, not an excuse to skip preparation.
The gospel will divide even families, with some members turning others over to persecutors.

f.w: the brother shall deliver up the brother

chapters.n: Disciples will be hated because they bear Christ’s name, but those who stay faithful to the end will be saved.

f.w: he that endureth to the end shall be saved

chapters.n: When persecuted, they may move on. Jesus adds a much-discussed saying: they won’t finish reaching Israel’s towns before the Son of Man comes.

f.w: till the Son of man be come
f.g: Interpreted variously — as Jesus coming to join them, his resurrection, Jerusalem’s fall, or his Second Coming.

chapters.n: Students don’t outrank their teacher. If Jesus was persecuted, his followers should expect the same.

f.w: The disciple is not above his master

chapters.n: If enemies called the Master “Beelzebub,” his servants shouldn’t be surprised at being slandered too.

f.g: A name for Satan; probably from Baal-zebub, a Philistine god, mocked as “lord of the flies.”
The head of the household — here Jesus himself.

chapters.n: Don’t be afraid of opponents. Truth will come out; everything hidden will eventually be revealed.

f.w: nothing covered, that shall not be revealed

chapters.n: What Jesus teaches them privately they must proclaim openly. Flat rooftops were places to make public announcements.
Persecutors can only kill the body. The One to revere is God, who has power over the eternal soul.

f.g: Here fear means deep reverence and awe for God, the final Judge.
Greek Gehenna — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a symbol of judgment.

chapters.n: Sparrows were among the cheapest things sold in the market, yet God notices even when one falls.

f.g: A small copper coin (Greek assarion), worth about 1/16 of a day’s wage.
Without your Father knowing or caring.

chapters.n: God knows us in astonishing detail — down to the number of hairs on our heads.

f.w: the very hairs of your head are all numbered

chapters.n: If God cares for sparrows, he surely cares for his children. That knowledge drives out fear.

f.w: ye are of more value than many sparrows

chapters.n: Those who openly stand up for Christ will find him standing up for them before the Father.

f.g: confess = openly acknowledge, declare loyalty.

chapters.n: The reverse is also true: to deny him before others is to cut ourselves off from his advocacy.
Jesus brings inner peace, but his message also divides — people will take sides for and against him.

f.g: A symbol of division, not literal violence. Luke has “division.”

chapters.n: Jesus quotes Micah to show how faith in him can split families when some accept and others oppose.

f.g: at variance = in conflict, divided.

chapters.n: Sometimes the hardest opposition comes from those closest to us.

f.w: a man's foes shall be they of his own household

chapters.n: Love for Christ must come before every other love, even family. Rightly ordered, that love strengthens our families rather than weakening them.

f.w: loveth father or mother more than me

chapters.n: Before his own crucifixion, Jesus says disciples must take up their cross — willing to bear sacrifice and even shame to follow him.

f.g: The JST of Matthew 16:26 explains taking up the cross as denying oneself all ungodliness and keeping the commandments.

chapters.n: A central paradox of discipleship: clinging to our own life loses it, but giving our life to Christ gains true, eternal life.

f.w: loseth his life for my sake shall find it

chapters.n: To welcome Christ’s messengers is to welcome Christ himself, and through him the Father who sent him.

f.w: He that receiveth you receiveth me

chapters.n: Those who support a prophet or righteous person because of who they are share in that person’s reward.

f.w: in the name of a prophet
f.g: Because he is a prophet.

chapters.n: Even the smallest kindness — a cup of cold water — given to a humble disciple will be remembered and rewarded by God.

f.g: Humble, ordinary disciples, not only children.

chapters.n: Having instructed the Twelve, Jesus continues his own preaching tour through the towns of Galilee.

f.w: when Jesus had made an end

chapters.n: John the Baptist is now in prison, arrested by Herod Antipas. Hearing reports about Jesus, he sends two of his disciples to him.

f.g: The historian Josephus places John’s imprisonment at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: The question — “Are you the one who is to come?” — may have been asked for his disciples’ sake, or out of John’s own struggle in prison. Either way, it is honest.

f.g: A title for the expected Messiah.

chapters.n: Instead of a simple yes, Jesus invites them to report what they themselves have heard and seen.

f.g: shew = show, tell.

chapters.n: His works echo Isaiah’s prophecies of what the Messiah would do. John, who knew those scriptures well, would understand the answer.

f.w: the poor have the gospel preached to them

chapters.n: A gentle blessing: happy is the person who doesn’t stumble over Jesus because he isn’t the kind of Messiah they expected.

f.g: Greek skandalizō — to stumble or be tripped up.

chapters.n: Now Jesus praises John. Did the crowds go into the desert to see someone flimsy, swaying with every breeze like the reeds along the Jordan? Certainly not.

f.w: A reed shaken with the wind
f.g: Reeds grew along the Jordan; the image means a weak, wavering person.

chapters.n: John was no pampered courtier in fine clothes. He wore camel’s hair and lived in the wilderness.

f.g: raiment = clothing; soft = luxurious.

chapters.n: John was a prophet — and more than a prophet, because he personally prepared the way for, and baptized, the Messiah.
Jesus identifies John as the messenger Malachi foretold, sent ahead to prepare the Lord’s way.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

chapters.n: No one born of a woman was greater than John. Yet the least in God’s kingdom is greater still. Joseph Smith taught that “he that is least” refers to Jesus himself.

f.w: he that is least in the kingdom of heaven
f.g: Joseph Smith explained this as Jesus, who was considered least by people of his day.

chapters.n: A difficult verse. Since John began preaching, God’s kingdom has faced violent opposition, with powerful people trying to seize or crush it.

f.g: suffereth = endures, undergoes. The Greek can also suggest the kingdom forcefully advancing.

f.w: the violent take it by force

chapters.n: The law and the prophets pointed forward to this moment. John was the last of the old prophetic order and the bridge to the new.
John fulfilled the role of the promised Elijah who would come before the Lord — a forerunner. Latter-day revelation also calls him an Elias.

f.g: Elias = Greek form of Elijah; also a title meaning a forerunner or preparer.

chapters.n: A call to pay close attention: those willing to understand should take this truth to heart.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear

chapters.n: Jesus compares his generation to children in the marketplace who complain that others won’t play their games.

f.g: The open marketplace, where children played.

chapters.n: Some children wanted to play “wedding,” others “funeral” — but nobody would join either game. People rejected both John and Jesus.

f.g: piped = played the flute, as at a wedding.
lamented = wailed in mourning.

chapters.n: John lived austerely, fasting and avoiding wine, and critics said he was demon-possessed.
Jesus ate with all kinds of people, and critics called him a glutton and drunkard. Still, true wisdom is proven by its results.

f.g: winebibber = heavy drinker.

f.w: wisdom is justified of her children
f.g: Wisdom is shown to be right by what it produces. Some manuscripts read “by her works.”

chapters.n: Jesus rebukes the towns that saw most of his miracles yet did not change their lives.

f.g: upbraid = scold, reproach.

chapters.n: Chorazin and Bethsaida were Jewish towns near the Sea of Galilee. Even pagan Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen such miracles.

f.g: A town a few miles north of Capernaum; its ruins still stand.
Phoenician port cities on the Mediterranean coast, often condemned by the prophets.
Rough goat-hair clothing and ashes — outward signs of mourning and repentance.

chapters.n: Greater light brings greater accountability. Those who saw more will be judged more strictly.
Capernaum, Jesus’s own home base and honored by his presence, will be humbled for its unbelief. Even Sodom would have repented.

f.g: Greek Hades — the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Sodom, the classic example of wickedness, will fare better in judgment than Capernaum, which saw Christ and still refused him.
Jesus thanks the Father that the truths of the kingdom are revealed to humble, childlike people rather than to the proud and self-sufficient.

f.g: Little children — the humble and teachable.
prudent = clever, worldly-wise.

chapters.n: Jesus accepts this as the Father’s good plan and wisdom.

f.w: so it seemed good in thy sight
f.g: This pleased you — it was your will.

chapters.n: The Father has entrusted all things to the Son. Only the Son truly knows the Father, and he reveals the Father to whomever he chooses.

f.w: All things are delivered unto me of my Father

f.g: save = except.

chapters.n: One of the most tender invitations in scripture. Jesus calls everyone worn out by burdens — sin, grief, rules, life — to come to him for rest.

f.g: Weighed down, like an overloaded animal.

chapters.n: A yoke joined two oxen to pull together. Jesus invites us to be yoked with him — to learn from him as he carries the load beside us.

f.g: A wooden beam fitted over the necks of draft animals; rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the law.”

chapters.n: His yoke fits well and his burden is light — not because discipleship is effortless, but because he shares the weight and gives strength.

f.g: easy = well-fitting, kind (Greek chrēstos).

chapters.n: Walking through grainfields on the Sabbath, Jesus’s hungry disciples pick heads of grain and eat. The law allowed this for travelers; the question was doing it on the Sabbath.

f.g: corn = grain, such as wheat or barley (not American maize).
an hungred = hungry.

chapters.n: The Pharisees count picking grain as harvesting — one of the kinds of work their traditions forbade on the Sabbath.

f.w: not lawful to do upon the sabbath day

chapters.n: Jesus answers from scripture, pointing to an episode in David’s life when he and his men were hungry.
David ate the holy bread from the sanctuary, normally reserved for priests. Human need was placed above ritual rule.

f.g: Twelve loaves set before the Lord in the sanctuary each Sabbath, later eaten by priests.

chapters.n: Priests work hard on the Sabbath — offering sacrifices — yet aren’t guilty, because their work serves God.

f.g: Technically break its rest by working.

chapters.n: A bold claim: something — someone — greater than the temple is present. If temple service justifies Sabbath work, how much more service to Jesus.
Jesus again quotes Hosea. Had the Pharisees understood that God prefers mercy, they wouldn’t have condemned innocent disciples.

f.w: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice

chapters.n: Jesus, as the Lord who gave the Sabbath, has authority to explain its true purpose.

f.w: Lord even of the sabbath day

chapters.n: Jesus enters a synagogue on the Sabbath — the setting for a second Sabbath controversy.

f.g: A local Jewish meeting place for prayer and scripture reading.

chapters.n: A man with a shriveled hand is there. Jesus’s critics use him as a test case, hoping to catch Jesus breaking their rules.

f.g: Shrunken and paralyzed.

chapters.n: Jesus points out their own practice: any of them would rescue a trapped sheep on the Sabbath.

f.w: lay hold on it, and lift it out

chapters.n: A person is worth far more than a sheep. So doing good — including healing — is right on the Sabbath.

f.w: it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days

chapters.n: Jesus simply tells the man to stretch out his hand, and as he obeys it is fully restored. Healing by a word involved no “work” at all.
Instead of rejoicing, the Pharisees begin plotting to kill Jesus — a sobering turning point.
Knowing their plot, Jesus withdraws, but crowds follow and he heals them all. Opposition doesn’t stop his compassion.
He asks those healed not to publicize him. He isn’t seeking fame or confrontation.
Matthew again explains Jesus’s quiet approach as fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of the Lord’s servant.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah.

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah 42: God’s chosen, beloved servant, filled with the Spirit, will bring justice even to the Gentiles. The words echo the Father’s voice at Jesus’s baptism.

f.g: Here: justice, right order.

chapters.n: The servant won’t be loud or quarrelsome, drawing attention to himself in the streets.

f.g: strive = quarrel, wrangle.

chapters.n: He is infinitely gentle: he won’t snap a bent reed or snuff out a flickering wick. He tenderly preserves those who are weak and nearly spent.

f.g: A lamp wick that is barely burning.

chapters.n: Even Gentile nations will put their hope in his name — a hint of the worldwide mission to come.

f.w: in his name shall the Gentiles trust

chapters.n: Jesus heals a man made blind and mute by an evil spirit, so that he both sees and speaks.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak.

chapters.n: The amazed crowd begins asking whether Jesus could be the Messiah, the promised son of David.

f.w: Is not this the son of David?

chapters.n: Unable to deny the miracle, the Pharisees claim Jesus works by Satan’s power.

f.w: Beelzebub the prince of the devils

chapters.n: Jesus exposes the flaw in their logic: any kingdom, city, or family fighting itself will collapse.
Why would Satan defeat his own servants? That would destroy his own kingdom.
Other Jewish exorcists also cast out spirits. If the Pharisees’ logic were applied to them, they’d be condemned too.

f.g: Your followers or people of your own group.

chapters.n: If Jesus casts out devils by God’s Spirit, then God’s kingdom has arrived in their midst.

f.g: Luke has “the finger of God,” recalling Exodus 8:19.

chapters.n: To rob a strong man, you must first tie him up. Jesus is overpowering Satan and freeing those Satan held captive.

f.g: spoil = plunder, carry off.

chapters.n: There is no neutral ground with Christ. Those who don’t help him gather people are, in effect, scattering them.

f.w: He that is not with me is against me

chapters.n: God forgives every kind of sin and even blasphemy if people repent — except blasphemy against the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Speaking against Jesus in ignorance can be forgiven. Latter-day Saint teaching explains the unpardonable sin as knowingly denying Christ after receiving a sure witness from the Holy Ghost.

f.w: neither in this world, neither in the world to come

chapters.n: Jesus returns to his tree image: be consistent. Good trees bear good fruit. His good works show where his power comes from.

f.w: the tree is known by his fruit

chapters.n: Words reveal the heart. The Pharisees’ slander came from what filled their hearts.

f.g: Offspring of snakes — the same rebuke John the Baptist used.

f.w: out of the abundance of the heart

chapters.n: Each heart is a storehouse. What we fill it with determines what we bring out.

f.g: A storeroom or treasury.

chapters.n: We are accountable for our words, even careless ones. Words matter because they flow from who we are.

f.g: A careless, useless, or harmful word.

chapters.n: Our words will be evidence in judgment — either declaring us righteous or condemning us.

f.g: justified = declared right, acquitted.

chapters.n: Right after this miracle, some scribes and Pharisees demand a sign — proof on their terms.
Jesus calls sign-seeking a mark of spiritual unfaithfulness. The only sign they’ll get is that of Jonah.

f.g: Unfaithful to God, as a spouse breaks a marriage covenant.
Jonas = Jonah.

chapters.n: Jonah’s three days inside the great fish foreshadow Jesus’s three days in the tomb before rising.

f.g: A Jewish way of reckoning that counted any part of a day as a day.
Greek kētos — a great sea creature.

chapters.n: Pagan Nineveh repented when Jonah preached. Jesus, far greater, preaches to Israel, which refuses to repent.
The queen of Sheba traveled far to hear Solomon’s wisdom. One far wiser than Solomon is here, and they won’t listen.

f.g: The queen of Sheba, probably from southern Arabia.

chapters.n: Jesus describes an evil spirit cast out of a person, wandering in desolate places and finding no rest.

f.g: Deserts, thought to be haunts of evil spirits.

chapters.n: Returning, the spirit finds its old “house” clean and tidy — but empty. Nothing good has moved in.

f.g: garnished = decorated, put in order.

chapters.n: It brings seven worse spirits, and the person ends up worse than before. Removing evil isn’t enough; we must fill our lives with God. Jesus applies this to his generation.

f.w: the last state of that man is worse than the first

chapters.n: Mary and Jesus’s brothers arrive and wait outside, wanting to speak with him.

f.g: Jesus’s younger half-brothers, sons of Mary and Joseph.
without = outside.

chapters.n: Someone passes the message along to Jesus.
Jesus uses the moment to teach — not rejecting his family, but redefining what family means in God’s kingdom.
Pointing to his disciples, he says these are his family too.

f.w: Behold my mother and my brethren!

chapters.n: Anyone who does the Father’s will becomes part of Jesus’s family — a bond as close as mother, brother, or sister.

f.w: whosoever shall do the will of my Father

chapters.n: The same day as the conflict in chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house and sits by the Sea of Galilee — the setting for his great sermon in parables.
The crowd is so large that Jesus teaches from a boat just offshore. Teachers usually sat to teach, and the water helped carry his voice.

f.w: he went into a ship, and sat

chapters.n: Jesus begins teaching in parables — stories from everyday life with a deeper spiritual meaning. The first is about a farmer sowing seed.

f.g: Greek parabolē — “to throw alongside”: a comparison that sets a familiar story beside a spiritual truth.

f.w: a sower went forth to sow

chapters.n: Farmers scattered seed by hand, so some landed on the hard, trampled path where birds quickly ate it.

f.g: fowls = birds.

chapters.n: Some fell on rocky ground with only a thin layer of soil. Those seeds sprouted quickly because the shallow soil warmed fast.

f.g: Limestone bedrock lying just under a thin layer of soil — common in Galilee.
forthwith = immediately.

chapters.n: But with no deep roots, the young plants withered in the hot sun.
Other seed fell among thorn roots. The thorns grew up with the grain and choked it out.

f.g: Thistles and weeds whose roots were already in the soil.

chapters.n: Some seed fell on good soil and produced an amazing harvest — thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown.
A call to listen closely. A parable rewards those who think about it and want to understand.
The disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables instead of speaking plainly.

f.w: Why speakest thou unto them in parables?

chapters.n: The disciples have been given to understand the “mysteries” of the kingdom — truths revealed to the faithful, not hidden secrets of a club.

f.g: Greek mystērion — truths knowable only by revelation.

chapters.n: A spiritual law: those who receive and use truth are given more; those who reject it lose even what they had.

f.w: whosoever hath, to him shall be given

f.g: The JST reads “whosoever continueth not to receive.”

chapters.n: Parables reveal truth to seekers but conceal it from those who have closed their minds. They look without truly seeing.
Jesus applies Isaiah’s prophecy about people who hear God’s word but won’t understand it.

f.w: By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand

chapters.n: The problem lies in the heart. People have grown dull and shut their eyes, so they don’t turn to God and receive healing.

f.g: waxed = grown, become; gross = thick, dull, insensitive.
converted = turned around, turned back to God.

chapters.n: The disciples are blessed because they are willing to see and hear.
Ancient prophets longed to witness the Messiah’s coming. The disciples are living it.

f.w: many prophets and righteous men have desired to see

chapters.n: Now Jesus privately explains the parable of the sower.
The path stands for those who hear but don’t understand. Satan quickly snatches the word away before it can take root.

f.g: Satan.

chapters.n: Rocky ground is the person who receives the word with instant joy — an enthusiastic but shallow start.

f.g: anon = immediately.

chapters.n: Without deep roots, that faith lasts only until trials come. Then the person stumbles and falls away.

f.g: dureth = endures, lasts.
by and by = soon, immediately.

chapters.n: Thorny ground pictures people whose worries and love of money crowd out the word until it bears no fruit.
Good ground is the person who hears, understands, and bears fruit. The harvest varies, but all are fruitful.
A new parable: the kingdom is like a farmer who plants good seed in his field.
At night an enemy secretly sows weeds among the wheat. Such sabotage was a known act of revenge in the ancient world.

f.g: Probably darnel, a poisonous weed that looks almost identical to wheat in its early growth.

chapters.n: Only when the grain begins to form does the difference become clear.

f.g: The green stalk.

chapters.n: Puzzled servants ask the owner how weeds got into a field sown with good seed.

f.g: The owner and master of the estate.

chapters.n: The owner knows an enemy did it. The servants offer to pull the weeds right away.
He says no. The roots are tangled, and pulling the weeds now would destroy the good wheat as well.

f.w: lest while ye gather up the tares

chapters.n: Both will grow until harvest, then be separated. Latter-day revelation and the JST reverse the order: the wheat is gathered first, then the tares burned.

f.w: Gather ye together first the tares
f.g: The JST reads “gather ye together first the wheat into my barn; and the tares are bound in bundles to be burned.”

chapters.n: The kingdom is like a mustard seed — tiny at the start, but it grows remarkably large.
The proverbially smallest seed becomes a large shrub where birds can nest. Christ’s kingdom begins small and grows to shelter many.

f.g: Garden plants.

chapters.n: A little yeast hidden in a large batch of dough silently works through the whole thing. The gospel quietly transforms people and the world.

f.g: Yeast or a bit of fermented dough used to make bread rise.
Roughly 40 liters of flour — enough bread to feed over a hundred people.

chapters.n: To the crowds Jesus now taught only in parables.

f.w: without a parable spake he not unto them

chapters.n: Matthew sees this as fulfilling a psalm in which the speaker opens his mouth in parables to reveal ancient truths.

f.w: I will open my mouth in parables
from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: In the house, away from the crowd, the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the wheat and tares.

f.g: Explain to us.

chapters.n: The sower of good seed is Jesus himself, the Son of Man.
The field is the whole world. The good seed are people who belong to God’s kingdom; the weeds are those who follow the evil one.
The devil sowed the weeds; the harvest is the end of the age; the reapers are angels.

f.g: The JST adds “or the destruction of the wicked.” Greek aiōn means age or era.

chapters.n: As weeds are gathered and burned, so will it be at the end of this age.
Angels will remove from Christ’s kingdom everything that causes sin and all who do evil.

f.g: Everything that causes people to stumble into sin.

chapters.n: Their fate is pictured as a blazing furnace — a symbol of the anguish of the wicked.
