The righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom — a beautiful image of glory.
A man stumbles on buried treasure, hides it again, and joyfully sells everything to buy the field. The kingdom is worth all we have.

f.g: With no banks, people often buried valuables in the ground for safekeeping.

chapters.n: A second picture of the same truth: a merchant actively searching for fine pearls.

f.g: goodly = fine, beautiful.

chapters.n: Finding one pearl of exceptional worth, he sells everything to buy it. The kingdom of God is worth any sacrifice.

f.g: The Pearl of Great Price, one of the Latter-day Saint standard works, takes its name from this parable.

chapters.n: The kingdom is like a dragnet pulled through the sea that catches all kinds of fish.

f.g: A dragnet, weighted at the bottom and floated at the top, drawn between boats or to shore.

chapters.n: Fishermen sort the catch, keeping the good and throwing out the bad (including fish forbidden under the law).
Like the wheat and tares, this pictures a final separation of the wicked from the righteous at the end of the age.

f.w: sever the wicked from among the just

f.g: sever = separate.

chapters.n: Jesus repeats the solemn warning about the furnace and the weeping of the lost.
Jesus checks for understanding. The disciples say yes.

f.w: Have ye understood all these things?
f.g: Understanding is the mark of “good ground” (v. 23).

chapters.n: A disciple trained in the kingdom is like a homeowner bringing out both new and old treasures — combining ancient scripture with Christ’s new revelation.
Having finished these parables, Jesus moves on — Matthew’s marker for the end of a major discourse.

f.w: when Jesus had finished these parables

chapters.n: Back in his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus teaches in the synagogue. People are amazed but puzzled about where he got such wisdom and power.

f.g: His hometown, Nazareth.

chapters.n: They know him as the carpenter’s son and know his whole family. Familiarity makes it hard to see him as anything more.

f.g: Greek tektōn — a builder who might work in wood or stone.

f.w: James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas
f.g: Jesus’s younger half-brothers; James and Judas (Jude) are traditionally linked to the epistles of James and Jude.

chapters.n: His sisters live there too. They think they know exactly who he is, so his greatness offends them.
They take offense. Jesus observes that prophets are honored everywhere except at home, where people think they know them best.

f.w: A prophet is not without honour

chapters.n: Because of their unbelief, Jesus did few miracles there. Miracles follow faith; they don’t force it.
Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, hears reports about Jesus’s growing fame.

f.g: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. Tetrarch = ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom.

chapters.n: His guilty conscience leads him to a fearful conclusion: Jesus must be John the Baptist come back from the dead.

f.w: he is risen from the dead

chapters.n: Matthew flashes back to explain. Herod had imprisoned John because of Herodias, who had left her husband, Herod’s half-brother, to marry Herod.

f.g: A granddaughter of Herod the Great; she married two of her uncles in turn.

chapters.n: John had boldly told Herod that this marriage broke God’s law. Prophets speak truth even to powerful rulers.

f.w: It is not lawful for thee to have her

chapters.n: Herod wanted John dead but feared a public backlash, since the people regarded John as a prophet.

f.w: they counted him as a prophet

chapters.n: At Herod’s birthday banquet, Herodias’s daughter danced for the guests and delighted Herod.

f.g: The historian Josephus names her Salome; she was probably a young teenager.

chapters.n: In a rash moment, Herod swore an oath to give her anything she asked.

f.g: Mark adds that he offered up to half his kingdom.

chapters.n: Prompted by her vengeful mother, she asks for John’s head on a platter — right then and there.

f.g: charger = a large serving platter.

f.w: being before instructed of her mother
f.g: Having been coached by her mother beforehand.

chapters.n: Herod is upset, but pride and fear of losing face before his guests win out over conscience. He grants the request.
John is beheaded in the prison — a martyr for speaking the truth.

f.g: Latter-day Saints believe the resurrected John restored the Aaronic Priesthood in 1829.

chapters.n: The horrifying “gift” is carried to the girl, who brings it to her mother.

f.g: damsel = a young girl.

chapters.n: John’s loyal disciples bury his body and then go tell Jesus, his cousin and the one John had prepared the way for.
Grieving the news, Jesus seeks solitude by boat. But crowds see where he’s going and hurry around the shore on foot.

f.g: A deserted, uninhabited area — not necessarily sandy desert. Luke places it near Bethsaida.

chapters.n: Though he wanted time alone, Jesus is moved with compassion when he sees the crowd and heals their sick.
As evening falls the disciples suggest sending everyone away to buy food in nearby villages.

f.g: victuals (pronounced “vittles”) = food.

chapters.n: Jesus surprises them: “You give them something to eat.” He invites them to be part of the solution.
All they have is five loaves and two fish — John’s Gospel says from a boy’s lunch.

f.g: Small flat barley loaves and probably dried or salted fish.

chapters.n: Jesus simply says, “Bring them to me.” What we offer him, however small, he can multiply.

f.g: hither = here.

chapters.n: Jesus has the people sit, gives thanks, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to distribute — actions that foreshadow the Last Supper.
Everyone eats until full, and twelve baskets of leftovers remain — more than they started with.

f.g: Possibly one for each apostle; twelve also recalls the tribes of Israel.

chapters.n: About 5,000 men were fed, plus women and children — perhaps well over ten thousand people. This is the only miracle besides the Resurrection recorded in all four Gospels.
Jesus immediately sends the disciples off by boat while he dismisses the crowd. John notes the people wanted to make him king by force.

f.g: constrained = urged strongly, made them.

chapters.n: Then Jesus climbs a mountain alone to pray, as he often did after demanding days.
Meanwhile the disciples’ boat is far from land, battered by waves and a strong headwind.

f.g: The wind was blowing against them.

chapters.n: Between 3 and 6 a.m., after hours of rowing, Jesus comes to them walking on the water.

f.w: the fourth watch of the night
f.g: Romans divided the night into four watches; the fourth ran roughly from 3 to 6 a.m.

chapters.n: Terrified, the disciples think they are seeing a ghost and scream in fear.

f.g: A ghost or apparition.

chapters.n: Jesus calms them at once: “Take courage; it is I; don’t be afraid.” The words “it is I” echo God’s name, “I AM.”

f.g: Greek egō eimi — literally “I am.”

chapters.n: Peter, bold as ever, asks Jesus to call him out onto the water.

f.g: bid = command, invite.

chapters.n: At Jesus’s word, Peter steps out of the boat and actually walks on water toward him.
When Peter shifts his focus from Jesus to the wind, fear takes over and he begins to sink. His three-word prayer is enough.

f.g: boisterous = strong, violent.

chapters.n: Jesus instantly reaches out and catches him. His gentle rebuke asks Peter to consider why he doubted.
As soon as they climb into the boat, the wind stops.
The disciples worship Jesus and declare that he truly is the Son of God — a major step in their understanding.

f.w: Of a truth thou art the Son of God

chapters.n: They land at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: A small fertile plain south of Capernaum; the lake itself was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret.

chapters.n: Local people recognize Jesus and quickly spread word, bringing all their sick to him.

f.g: Recognized him.

chapters.n: Like the woman in chapter 9, they ask only to touch the edge of his cloak — and all who do are healed.

f.g: Completely healed.

chapters.n: Religious experts travel all the way from Jerusalem to Galilee to investigate Jesus — a sign that the leaders are watching him closely.
They accuse Jesus’s disciples of skipping the ritual hand-washing before meals. This was about ceremonial purity, not hygiene.

f.g: Oral rules handed down by earlier rabbis, meant to “fence” the law of Moses; later written in the Mishnah.

chapters.n: Jesus turns the question around: their traditions actually break God’s commandments.

f.g: transgress = break, step over a boundary.

chapters.n: He cites the Ten Commandments: honor your parents. The law treated cursing parents as a capital crime.
Their tradition let a person declare property a “gift” dedicated to God, so it couldn’t be used to support aging parents.

f.g: Mark uses the Hebrew term Corban — something vowed to God.

chapters.n: This loophole freed people from caring for their parents. A human rule had canceled out God’s clear command.

f.g: Made void, cancelled.

chapters.n: Jesus calls them hypocrites and says Isaiah described them perfectly long ago.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah.

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah: people honor God with their words while their hearts are far from him.

f.w: This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth

chapters.n: Worship becomes empty when human rules are taught as if they were God’s commandments.

f.g: Pointlessly, without effect.

chapters.n: Jesus now turns to the crowd with an important teaching.
What makes a person spiritually unclean isn’t food going in, but what comes out — words and actions flowing from the heart.

f.g: defile = make unclean, spiritually polluted.

f.w: that which cometh out of the mouth

chapters.n: The disciples warn Jesus that he has offended the Pharisees.

f.g: Greek skandalizō — caused to stumble, scandalized.

chapters.n: Teachings and leaders not rooted in God will eventually be pulled up like weeds.

f.w: Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted

chapters.n: Leave them be: they are blind guides leading blind followers, and both will end up in the pit.

f.g: A pit — perhaps an open well or cistern.

chapters.n: Peter asks Jesus to explain this saying, which he calls a parable.
Jesus is surprised that even his close disciples still don’t understand.
Food simply passes through the body; it doesn’t touch the heart.

f.g: draught = latrine, toilet.

chapters.n: Words and deeds, on the other hand, reveal and come from the heart.
Jesus lists the evils that begin in the heart. Notice that sinful actions start as sinful thoughts.

f.g: Sexual relations outside of marriage.

chapters.n: These are what truly make a person unclean before God — not eating with unwashed hands.

f.g: unwashen = unwashed.

chapters.n: Jesus travels northwest into Gentile territory near the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon.

f.g: coasts = region, borders.

chapters.n: A Gentile woman pleads with Jesus to free her tormented daughter. Surprisingly, she calls him “Son of David,” a title many in Israel wouldn’t use.

f.g: A Gentile; Mark calls her a Greek of Syrophenician birth. Canaanites were Israel’s ancient enemies.
Severely tormented.

chapters.n: At first Jesus says nothing. The disciples urge him to send her away because her pleading is embarrassing them.

f.w: he answered her not a word
f.g: His silence seems to test and draw out her faith.

chapters.n: Jesus explains that his mortal mission was first to Israel. The gospel would go to the Gentiles later.

f.w: the lost sheep of the house of Israel

chapters.n: Undeterred, she kneels before him and simply begs, “Lord, help me.”
Jesus uses a common saying: food for the children shouldn’t be given to the dogs. Israel had the first claim. His word for “dogs” is the softer word for household pets.

f.g: meet = right, fitting.
Greek kynaria — little dogs, house pets.

chapters.n: Her quick, humble answer accepts his words and finds hope in them: even pets get the crumbs that fall from the table.

f.g: Yes, Lord — that is true.

chapters.n: Jesus praises her great faith and heals her daughter at that moment. A Gentile woman becomes a model of persistent faith.
Returning to the Sea of Galilee, Jesus climbs a hillside and sits down to teach.

f.w: came nigh unto the sea of Galilee
f.g: Mark says through the Decapolis, the largely Gentile region east of the lake.

chapters.n: Huge crowds bring the disabled and sick and lay them at his feet, and he heals them.

f.g: maimed = crippled, missing or injured in a limb.

chapters.n: The people are amazed and praise “the God of Israel” — a phrase suggesting many of them were Gentiles.

f.w: they glorified the God of Israel

chapters.n: After three days with him, the people have no food. Jesus is concerned they’ll collapse on the way home.

f.g: Here simply: without food.

f.w: lest they faint in the way

chapters.n: The disciples wonder where they could find enough bread in such a remote place — even though they saw the 5,000 fed.

f.g: whence = from where.

chapters.n: They have seven loaves and a few small fish.

f.g: Seven often symbolizes completeness in scripture.

chapters.n: Jesus has the crowd sit down on the ground.
As before, Jesus gives thanks, breaks the bread, and has his disciples distribute it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō — the root of “Eucharist.”

chapters.n: All eat their fill, and seven large baskets of leftovers are gathered.

f.g: meat = food; broken pieces of bread.
A different word than in 14:20 — large hampers, like the one Paul was later lowered in.

chapters.n: About 4,000 men, plus women and children, are fed — a second, separate miracle of abundance.
Jesus sends the crowd home and sails to Magdala on the western shore — likely the hometown of Mary Magdalene.

f.g: Some manuscripts read Magadan; Mark has Dalmanutha.

chapters.n: Two rival groups, the Pharisees and Sadducees, unite against Jesus. They demand a sign from heaven, hoping to trap or discredit him.

f.g: A priestly, aristocratic party tied to the temple; they rejected the resurrection and oral traditions.
Testing, trying to trap him.

chapters.n: Jesus points to weather lore everyone knew: a red evening sky promises good weather.

f.g: Similar to the saying “Red sky at night, sailor’s delight.”

chapters.n: A red, overcast morning sky warns of a storm. They read the sky well but miss the obvious signs that the Messiah is among them.

f.g: lowring (lowering) = dark, gloomy, threatening.

chapters.n: As in chapter 12, the only sign given will be Jonah’s — Jesus’s death and resurrection after three days. Then he leaves them.

f.w: the sign of the prophet Jonas

chapters.n: Crossing the lake again, the disciples realize they forgot to bring bread.

f.g: Mark notes they had only one loaf in the boat.

chapters.n: Jesus warns them to beware the “leaven” of the Pharisees and Sadducees — a metaphor for something small that spreads and corrupts.

f.g: Yeast; often a symbol of corrupting influence.

chapters.n: The disciples take him literally and think he is scolding them for forgetting bread.

f.g: Discussed among themselves.

chapters.n: Jesus gently rebukes their small faith. Worrying about bread with him in the boat shows they still don’t trust him fully.
He reminds them of feeding the 5,000 with five loaves and the twelve baskets left over.

f.w: the five loaves of the five thousand

chapters.n: And the 4,000 fed with seven loaves, with seven baskets left over. Lack of bread is no problem for him.

f.w: the seven loaves of the four thousand

chapters.n: Jesus asks how they could miss that he wasn’t talking about literal bread at all.

f.w: I spake it not to you concerning bread

chapters.n: Finally they understand: the “leaven” was the false teaching and influence of the religious leaders.

f.g: doctrine = teaching.

chapters.n: At Caesarea Philippi, far north near Mount Hermon, Jesus asks what people are saying about who he is.

f.g: A city near the headwaters of the Jordan, rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip; home to a shrine of the god Pan.

chapters.n: Popular opinion sees him as a great prophet returned — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or another.

f.g: Elias = Elijah.
Jeremias = Jeremiah.

chapters.n: Then the personal question that every disciple must answer: “But who do you say that I am?”

f.w: But whom say ye that I am?

chapters.n: Peter answers boldly: Jesus is the Christ, the promised Messiah, and the Son of the living God.

f.g: Greek Christos = Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah), “the Anointed One.”

f.w: the Son of the living God

chapters.n: Jesus blesses Peter and explains that this knowledge came by revelation from the Father, not from human reasoning.

f.g: Aramaic for “son of Jonah” (or John).

f.w: flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee

chapters.n: A play on words: Peter (Petros) means “rock.” Joseph Smith taught that the rock on which Christ builds his Church is revelation, and the powers of hell will not overcome it.

f.g: Greek petra — bedrock.
The power of death and the forces of evil.

chapters.n: Jesus promises Peter the keys of the kingdom — the authority to direct God’s work, so that what is sealed on earth is sealed in heaven.
Jesus tells them not to announce publicly that he is the Messiah yet, since many expected a political liberator.
A turning point: Jesus now begins teaching plainly that he must suffer, die in Jerusalem, and rise on the third day.

f.w: From that time forth began Jesus
be raised again the third day

chapters.n: Peter, who just confessed Jesus as Messiah, pulls him aside and insists this must never happen. A suffering Messiah didn’t fit his expectations.

f.g: Literally “God be merciful to you” — meaning “God forbid!”

chapters.n: Jesus sternly rebukes Peter. Discouraging the Savior from the Atonement echoes Satan’s temptations. Peter is thinking like a man, not like God.

f.g: savourest = have a taste for, are mindful of.
A stumbling block.

chapters.n: To follow Jesus means denying ourselves and taking up our cross. The JST explains this as denying ourselves ungodliness and every worldly lust and keeping his commandments.
Grasping at life on our own terms leads to losing it; giving our life to Christ is how we truly find it.

f.w: lose his life for my sake shall find it

chapters.n: Nothing in the world is worth trading for our soul. Its value is beyond any price.

f.w: gain the whole world, and lose his own soul

chapters.n: Christ will return in glory with his angels and judge each person according to what they have done.

f.w: reward every man according to his works

chapters.n: Some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom before dying — perhaps fulfilled days later at the Transfiguration. Latter-day revelation adds that John the Beloved was allowed to remain on earth.
Six days after Peter’s confession, Jesus takes his three closest apostles up a high mountain. The same three will later be with him in Gethsemane.

f.g: Traditionally Mount Tabor; many scholars suggest Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi.

chapters.n: Jesus is transfigured — his divine glory shines through. His face blazes like the sun and his clothing becomes brilliant white.

f.g: Greek metamorphoō — changed in form or appearance.
raiment = clothing.

chapters.n: Moses (representing the law) and Elijah (representing the prophets) appear and speak with Jesus — Luke says about his coming death in Jerusalem.

f.g: Elias = Elijah. Latter-day Saints believe these two conferred priesthood keys on Peter, James, and John here, as they later did in the Kirtland Temple.

chapters.n: Overwhelmed, Peter offers to build three shelters. He wants to hold on to this glorious moment.

f.g: Booths or tents, like those used at the Feast of Tabernacles.

chapters.n: A bright cloud — a sign of God’s presence — surrounds them, and the Father’s voice declares Jesus his beloved Son, as at his baptism, adding “hear ye him.”
Hearing God’s voice, the apostles fall face down in awe and fear.

f.g: sore = greatly, intensely.

chapters.n: Jesus gently touches them and tells them to get up and not be afraid.
When they look up, only Jesus remains. The law and the prophets give way to him alone.

f.g: save = except.

chapters.n: Coming down, Jesus tells them to keep the vision secret until after his resurrection, when it could be properly understood.

f.w: Tell the vision to no man

chapters.n: Having just seen Elijah, the disciples ask about the scribes’ teaching that Elijah must come before the Messiah.
Jesus affirms that Elijah will indeed come and restore all things — a prophecy Latter-day Saints see fulfilled in part in 1836.
Yet in another sense Elias had already come in John the Baptist, and he was rejected and killed. Jesus would suffer the same.

f.g: listed = wished, pleased.

chapters.n: The disciples realize he means John the Baptist, the forerunner who came in the spirit and power of Elijah.
Back at the foot of the mountain, a desperate father kneels before Jesus.
His son suffers violent seizures that throw him into fire and water. Mark describes the cause as an evil spirit.

f.g: Greek selēniazomai — literally “moonstruck”; it described seizures, which people then linked to the moon.
Severely tormented.

chapters.n: The disciples left behind had tried and failed to heal the boy.
Jesus expresses sorrow at the faithlessness he finds, then asks for the boy to be brought to him.

f.g: Twisted, turned from the right way.
suffer = bear with, put up with.

chapters.n: Jesus rebukes the evil spirit, and the boy is healed at once.
Privately, the disciples ask why their attempt failed.

f.g: Privately, away from the crowd.

chapters.n: Their faith was too weak. Even faith as small as a mustard seed, if genuine and growing, can move mountains.

f.w: faith as a grain of mustard seed

chapters.n: Some challenges require the extra spiritual power that comes through prayer and fasting.

f.g: Some ancient manuscripts lack this verse; Mark 9:29 contains the same teaching.
howbeit = however.

chapters.n: In Galilee, Jesus again predicts that he will be betrayed into human hands.

f.g: Greek paradidōmi — handed over, delivered up.

chapters.n: He foretells his death and resurrection on the third day. The disciples are deeply grieved, hearing the death more clearly than the rising.

f.w: the third day he shall be raised again

chapters.n: In Capernaum, collectors of the annual temple tax ask Peter whether Jesus pays it.

f.g: The half-shekel temple tax every Jewish man paid yearly for the temple’s upkeep.

chapters.n: Peter says yes. Before Peter can mention it, Jesus raises the question: do kings tax their own sons or others?

f.g: prevented = went before him, spoke first.
custom = duties, tolls.

chapters.n: Kings tax outsiders, not their own children. As God’s Son, Jesus owes no tax to his Father’s house.
Still, to avoid giving needless offense, Jesus sends Peter fishing. The first fish holds a coin worth exactly the tax for both of them.

f.g: Greek statēr — a coin worth four drachmas, exactly two half-shekel taxes.

chapters.n: This chapter is Matthew’s fourth major discourse, on life in the community of disciples. It begins with the disciples asking who will rank highest in God’s kingdom.
Jesus answers with an object lesson: he calls a small child and places the child in the middle of the group.

f.g: Children had little status in that society — which is the point.

chapters.n: Unless we change and become like little children — humble, trusting, teachable — we won’t enter the kingdom at all, let alone be great in it.

f.g: Turned around, changed.

chapters.n: True greatness in God’s kingdom is humility, the opposite of the status-seeking in the disciples’ question.
Welcoming a humble child for Jesus’s sake is welcoming Jesus himself.
Leading a believing “little one” into sin is so serious that drowning with a heavy millstone around one’s neck would be preferable.

f.g: Here: cause to stumble into sin or lose faith.
A large grinding stone turned by a donkey — far heavier than a hand mill.

chapters.n: In a fallen world temptations will come, but the person who causes them bears responsibility.

f.g: It is inevitable.

chapters.n: Vivid exaggeration: whatever leads you into sin, remove it decisively. Being spiritually whole is worth any sacrifice.

f.g: halt = lame, crippled.

chapters.n: Even the eye — what we choose to look at — must be guarded if it leads us into sin.

f.g: Literally “the Gehenna of fire.”

chapters.n: Never look down on these little ones; they are so precious that their angels have direct access to the Father.

f.g: despise = look down on, treat as worthless.

chapters.n: Jesus came specifically to rescue the lost. (Some ancient manuscripts lack this verse; a similar line appears in Luke 19:10.)

f.w: to save that which was lost

chapters.n: A shepherd with a hundred sheep goes searching the hills for the one that wandered off.
Finding it brings special joy. Every individual matters to God.

f.w: he rejoiceth more of that sheep

chapters.n: The Father doesn’t want even one of his little ones to be lost.
When someone wrongs you, go privately and talk with them first. The goal is reconciliation — “gaining” your brother — not winning.

f.g: Sin against you, wrong you.

chapters.n: If that fails, bring one or two others along, following the law’s principle of multiple witnesses.
If the person still won’t listen, bring it to the congregation. If they reject even that, they place themselves outside the fellowship.

f.g: Greek ekklēsia — the congregation of believers.
A Gentile, an outsider to the covenant.

chapters.n: Jesus extends to the apostles the binding and loosing authority promised to Peter — their decisions, made with his authority, are honored in heaven.

f.w: Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth

chapters.n: When disciples unite in prayer for something, the Father hears and answers.

f.w: if two of you shall agree

chapters.n: Even the smallest gathering in Christ’s name has his presence.

f.w: where two or three are gathered together in my name

chapters.n: Peter asks how many times he must forgive someone. Seven times seemed generous — some rabbis taught three.
Jesus answers: seventy times seven — in other words, without keeping count.

f.g: Possibly “seventy-seven times”; either way, limitless. It reverses Lamech’s boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge.

chapters.n: Jesus tells a parable about a king settling accounts with his servants.

f.g: Settle accounts, audit.

chapters.n: One servant owes ten thousand talents — an impossibly huge sum, deliberately exaggerated. It pictures our unpayable debt to God.

f.g: A talent was about 6,000 days’ wages; this debt equals roughly 60 million days of labor.

chapters.n: Unable to pay, he faces being sold with his family into slavery — a real practice for debts in the ancient world.

f.g: Since, because.

chapters.n: The servant begs for patience and promises to repay everything — something he could never actually do.

f.g: A desperate, impossible promise.

chapters.n: Moved with compassion, the king doesn’t just extend the deadline — he cancels the entire debt. That is grace.
The forgiven servant then finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii — real money, but tiny by comparison — and starts choking him.

f.g: A hundred denarii; a denarius was a day’s wage — roughly 600,000 times less than his own debt.

chapters.n: The fellow servant pleads with nearly the same words the first servant had used.
He refuses and has the man jailed until he pays, forgetting the mercy he himself just received.

f.g: Debtors’ prison; family or friends might raise money to free the prisoner.

chapters.n: The other servants are distressed and report everything to the king.

f.g: They were deeply grieved.

chapters.n: The king summons him and calls him wicked: he was forgiven everything simply because he asked.

f.g: Because you begged me.

chapters.n: The key question of the parable: having received such mercy, shouldn’t he show mercy too?

f.w: even as I had pity on thee

chapters.n: The angry king hands him over to the jailers until his debt is paid — which can never happen.

f.g: wroth = very angry.
Jailers or torturers.

chapters.n: Jesus applies it plainly: if we won’t forgive others from the heart, we cut ourselves off from God’s forgiveness.
Jesus’s Galilean ministry ends. He travels south toward Jerusalem by way of Perea, the region east of the Jordan — the beginning of his final journey.

f.w: when Jesus had finished these sayings

f.g: The region of Perea, east of the Jordan River, ruled by Herod Antipas.

chapters.n: Large crowds follow him there too, and he heals them.
Pharisees test him with a hot debate of the day: may a man divorce his wife for any reason at all? Rabbinic schools disagreed sharply on this.

f.g: put away = divorce.
The school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any reason; the school of Shammai only for serious sexual misconduct.

chapters.n: Jesus goes back past Moses to the Creation: God made humanity male and female from the beginning.
Quoting Genesis, Jesus shows marriage as God’s design: a man leaves his parents, is joined to his wife, and the two become one.

f.g: cleave = cling to, be joined to.
twain = two.

chapters.n: Marriage is a union God himself creates, so people should not tear it apart.

f.g: asunder = apart; separate, split.

f.w: What therefore God hath joined together

chapters.n: They counter: then why did Moses allow divorce with a written certificate?
Moses permitted divorce as a concession to hard hearts, not as God’s ideal. The original design was lifelong union.

f.g: suffered = allowed.

chapters.n: Jesus sets a higher standard: divorcing and remarrying, except for sexual unfaithfulness, is a form of adultery.

f.g: Greek porneia — sexual immorality.

chapters.n: The disciples, shocked by such a high standard, wonder whether it’s better not to marry at all.

f.w: it is not good to marry

chapters.n: Jesus says not everyone can accept the alternative of not marrying — only those given that ability.

f.w: save they to whom it is given
f.g: save = except.

chapters.n: Some can’t marry by birth, some because others made them eunuchs, and some choose celibacy to serve God. Latter-day Saint teaching holds eternal marriage central to God’s plan.

f.g: Men who were castrated or unable to father children; here also those who stay unmarried.

f.w: for the kingdom of heaven's sake

chapters.n: Parents bring their children for Jesus to bless, but the disciples scold them, thinking Jesus is too busy.
Jesus welcomes the children. God’s kingdom belongs to the childlike.

f.g: suffer = allow, let.

f.w: of such is the kingdom of heaven

chapters.n: Jesus places his hands on them in blessing, then continues his journey.
A man (vv. 20, 22 call him young and rich) asks what good deed will earn him eternal life.

f.w: what good thing shall I do

chapters.n: Jesus redirects him: true goodness comes from God alone. Then he points him to the commandments.

f.w: there is none good but one, that is, God

chapters.n: The man asks which ones. Jesus lists commandments from the second tablet — about how we treat others.
He adds honoring parents and the great summary: love your neighbor as yourself.

f.w: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

chapters.n: The young man sincerely says he has kept these all his life, yet he senses something is still missing.

f.g: Mark adds that Jesus, looking at him, loved him.

chapters.n: Jesus invites him to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow him. His wealth was the one thing standing between him and full discipleship.

f.g: perfect = complete, whole (Greek teleios).

chapters.n: He leaves sad. He has great wealth and isn’t willing to give it up — a sobering picture of a good person who stops short.
Jesus tells his disciples that wealth makes entering God’s kingdom very hard.

f.g: hardly = with great difficulty.

chapters.n: A deliberately absurd image: the largest animal in the region squeezing through the smallest opening. Trusting in riches makes salvation humanly impossible.

f.g: A literal sewing needle; the image is meant to sound impossible.

chapters.n: The disciples are stunned. Many assumed wealth was a sign of God’s favor — so if the rich can’t be saved, who can?
Jesus answers that salvation is impossible by human effort but possible with God. It is ultimately his gift.

f.w: with God all things are possible

chapters.n: Peter points out that the apostles have left everything to follow Jesus. What will they receive?
In the coming renewal of all things, the Twelve will sit on thrones judging Israel’s twelve tribes. Latter-day revelation confirms this role.

f.g: The rebirth or renewal of the world at Christ’s coming.

f.w: judging the twelve tribes of Israel

chapters.n: Whatever disciples give up for Christ — homes, family, land — they will receive back many times over, plus eternal life.
God’s kingdom reverses worldly rankings. Those who seem first now may end up last, and the reverse. The next parable illustrates this.

f.w: many that are first shall be last

chapters.n: Continuing his answer to Peter, Jesus tells a parable about a landowner hiring workers for his vineyard at daybreak, around 6 a.m.

f.g: The owner of an estate.
A common image for God’s people or work.

chapters.n: He agrees to pay them a denarius for the day — the normal fair wage for a laborer.

f.g: A denarius, a Roman silver coin — a standard day’s wage.

chapters.n: Around 9 a.m. he sees others standing around in the marketplace, where day laborers waited to be hired.

f.g: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about 9 a.m.

chapters.n: He hires them without naming a wage, simply promising to pay what is right. They trust him and go.

f.g: Whatever is fair.

chapters.n: He does the same at noon and again at 3 p.m.

f.g: About noon and 3 p.m.

chapters.n: At 5 p.m., with just an hour left, he finds still more people with no work and asks why they’ve been idle all day.

f.g: About 5 p.m. — the origin of the phrase “at the eleventh hour.”

chapters.n: No one had hired them. He sends them into the vineyard too. In God’s work, latecomers are still welcomed.
At evening the owner has his manager pay everyone, starting with those hired last — as the law required, wages were paid daily.

f.g: A manager who handled the owner’s business.

chapters.n: The one-hour workers each receive a full day’s wage — remarkable generosity.

f.g: A full denarius for one hour of work.

chapters.n: The all-day workers expect more, but they receive exactly what they agreed to.

f.w: they supposed that they should have received more
f.g: Comparison turned their fair wage into a grievance.

chapters.n: They grumble against the owner.

f.g: murmured = grumbled, complained.
The master of the household.

chapters.n: Their complaint: the latecomers did one hour, yet they’re treated the same as those who sweated through the heat of the whole day.

f.g: wrought = worked.

f.w: the burden and heat of the day
f.g: The scorching midday heat; a hot east wind could make field work grueling.

chapters.n: The owner calls the complainer “friend” and points out that he was paid exactly what was agreed. No injustice was done.

f.w: Friend, I do thee no wrong

chapters.n: The owner chooses to be generous to the latecomers, and that is his right.

f.g: Take what is yours.

chapters.n: The real issue is envy: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” God’s grace to others takes nothing from us.

f.g: An idiom for envy or stinginess.

chapters.n: In God’s kingdom the last are first. Many are invited, but few respond and become chosen.

f.w: many be called, but few chosen

chapters.n: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside privately.

f.g: Jerusalem sits high in the hills, so travelers always went “up” to it.

chapters.n: For the third time, Jesus predicts what awaits him: betrayal to the religious leaders and a death sentence.

f.w: they shall condemn him to death

chapters.n: This time he gives details: he will be handed to Gentiles (the Romans), mocked, whipped, and crucified — then rise on the third day.

f.g: The first time Matthew records Jesus naming crucifixion as the manner of his death.

f.w: the third day he shall rise again

chapters.n: Right after this solemn prediction, the mother of James and John comes with her sons to ask a favor.

f.g: Possibly Salome, who may have been Mary’s sister — making James and John Jesus’s cousins.

chapters.n: She asks for her sons to have the highest places of honor in his kingdom, at his right and left.

f.g: The place of greatest honor and authority.

f.w: Grant that these my two sons may sit

chapters.n: Jesus says they don’t understand what they’re asking. Can they drink his “cup” of suffering? They confidently say yes.

f.w: the cup that I shall drink of
f.g: A symbol of suffering assigned by God.

chapters.n: They will share his suffering — James became the first apostle martyred, and John suffered much. But places of honor are the Father’s to give.

f.w: Ye shall drink indeed of my cup

chapters.n: The other ten apostles are angry with James and John — perhaps because they wanted those places themselves.

f.g: Anger at something felt to be unfair.

chapters.n: Jesus contrasts worldly rulers, who lord it over their subjects, with the way his kingdom works.

f.g: Rulers.

chapters.n: Among his followers, whoever wants to be great must serve others.

f.g: Greek diakonos — servant, attendant (root of “deacon”).

chapters.n: Whoever wants to be first must become a servant to all.

f.g: Greek doulos — a slave or bondservant.

chapters.n: Jesus himself is the model: he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom — the price paid to set many free.

f.g: ransom = the price paid to free a slave or captive.

chapters.n: Leaving Jericho on the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus is followed by a large crowd, likely fellow pilgrims heading to Passover.

f.g: An oasis city about 15 miles northeast of Jerusalem, some 3,000 feet lower in elevation.

chapters.n: Two blind men by the roadside shout to Jesus as the Son of David — the messianic King.

f.g: Mark and Luke focus on one; Mark names him Bartimaeus.

chapters.n: The crowd tells them to be quiet, but they cry out even louder. Persistent faith won’t be silenced.

f.g: Be quiet.

chapters.n: Jesus stops, calls them, and asks what they want — inviting them to put their faith into words.

f.w: What will ye that I shall do unto you?

chapters.n: They ask simply to see. Unlike James and John’s request for status, theirs is humble.

f.w: that our eyes may be opened

chapters.n: Moved with compassion, Jesus touches their eyes. They see at once — and use their new sight to follow him.
The final week begins. Near Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, Jesus sends two disciples ahead on an errand.

f.g: A small village on the Mount of Olives; the name means “house of unripe figs.”
A ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, with a view over the temple.

chapters.n: He tells them they’ll find a donkey tied up with her colt, and to bring both. Jesus knows exactly what they will find.

f.g: Opposite you, just ahead.

f.w: an ass tied, and a colt with her

chapters.n: If anyone objects, they need only say “The Lord needs them,” and the owner will send them.

f.g: ought = anything.

chapters.n: Matthew explains that this happened to fulfill prophecy.
Quoting Zechariah: Zion’s King comes humbly on a donkey. Kings rode warhorses to battle but donkeys in peace; Jesus comes as a king of peace.

f.g: Sion = Zion; a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

f.w: Behold, thy King cometh unto thee

chapters.n: The disciples obey exactly.
They bring the animals and lay their cloaks on them as a saddle, and Jesus sits on them.

f.g: Spreading cloaks was a sign of royal honor.

chapters.n: The crowd spreads cloaks and branches on the road — a red-carpet welcome for a king. John says palm branches, giving us “Palm Sunday.”

f.g: strawed = strewed, scattered.

chapters.n: Crowds shout “Hosanna” and words from Psalm 118, a psalm sung at Passover. They openly hail Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of David.

f.g: Hebrew “Save, we pray!” — it became a shout of praise.

chapters.n: The whole city is stirred, asking “Who is this?” — the question Matthew’s Gospel has been answering all along.

f.g: moved = stirred up, shaken, like an earthquake (Greek seiō).

chapters.n: The crowd answers that he is the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.
Jesus drives the merchants and moneychangers out of the temple courts. Their business, in the court open to Gentiles, had turned worship into commerce.

f.g: They exchanged pilgrims’ coins for the approved currency used to pay the temple tax, often at a profit.
Doves were the sacrifice of the poor.

chapters.n: He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: God’s house is meant for prayer, but they’ve made it a hideout for robbers.

f.w: My house shall be called the house of prayer

chapters.n: With the commerce cleared away, the blind and the lame — once excluded from parts of the temple — come to Jesus, and he heals them.
The chief priests and scribes are furious at his miracles and at children shouting praise to the Son of David in the temple.

f.g: Greatly indignant.
The high priest and leading priestly families who controlled the temple.

chapters.n: Jesus answers with Psalm 8: God has ordained praise from the mouths of children. The children see what the leaders miss.

f.w: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings

f.g: Nursing infants.

chapters.n: Jesus spends the night in Bethany, about two miles away, likely with Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.

f.g: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives.
Stayed overnight.

chapters.n: Returning to the city the next morning, Jesus is hungry.

f.g: A reminder of his real humanity.

chapters.n: He finds a fig tree full of leaves but no fruit, and curses it; it withers. It acts out a parable about religion that looks good but bears no fruit.

f.g: Fig trees with leaves usually showed early fruit buds as well.
presently = immediately.

chapters.n: The disciples are amazed at how fast it withered.

f.g: How quickly.

chapters.n: Jesus turns the moment into a lesson on faith: faith without doubt can do even greater things, like moving a mountain into the sea.

f.w: If ye have faith, and doubt not

chapters.n: Whatever they ask in prayer, believing, they will receive — prayer offered in faith and in harmony with God’s will.
In the temple the leaders challenge Jesus: by what authority does he act — cleansing the temple and teaching there?

f.w: By what authority doest thou these things?

f.g: Lay leaders who sat with the priests on the Sanhedrin council.

chapters.n: Jesus responds, as rabbis often did, with a question of his own.

f.w: I also will ask you one thing
f.g: Answering a question with a question was a common rabbinic teaching method.

chapters.n: Was John’s baptism from God or from men? They realize that if they say “from heaven,” Jesus will ask why they didn’t believe John.

f.g: whence = from where.
“Heaven” was a respectful way of saying “God.”

chapters.n: But if they say “from men,” the crowd, who revere John as a prophet, will turn on them.

f.w: all hold John as a prophet

chapters.n: So they dodge with “We don’t know.” Since they won’t answer honestly, Jesus declines to answer them. The answer is implied: his authority, like John’s, comes from God.

f.g: We don’t know — an evasive answer.

chapters.n: Jesus tells a parable: a father asks his first son to work in the vineyard that day.
The son refuses, but later changes his mind and goes.

f.g: repented = changed his mind and turned around.

chapters.n: The second son politely agrees — then never goes.

f.w: I go, sir: and went not

chapters.n: Which son obeyed? The first. Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes, who repented, are entering God’s kingdom ahead of these religious leaders.

f.g: Which of the two.
harlots = prostitutes.

chapters.n: Notorious sinners believed John and repented; the leaders saw that change and still refused to believe.
Another parable, drawn from Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard: an owner plants a vineyard with every care and rents it to tenant farmers.

f.g: husbandmen = tenant farmers.
A watchtower for guarding the crop.

chapters.n: At harvest he sends servants to collect his share of the fruit.

f.g: The owner’s rightful portion of the crop.

chapters.n: The tenants beat, kill, and stone his servants — a picture of how Israel often treated the prophets.
He sends more servants, and they are treated the same way.

f.g: A larger group of servants.

chapters.n: Finally he sends his own son, sure they’ll respect him — a clear reference to Jesus himself.

f.g: reverence = respect.

chapters.n: The tenants see the heir and plot to kill him to seize the inheritance.
They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him — foreshadowing Jesus’s death outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

chapters.n: Jesus asks his listeners what the owner will do when he comes.

f.g: The owner.

chapters.n: The leaders answer, condemning themselves: he will destroy the wicked tenants and rent the vineyard to others who will give him its fruit.

f.w: render him the fruits in their seasons
f.g: render = give, pay.

chapters.n: Jesus quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders threw away has become the cornerstone. He is that rejected stone.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in the building.

chapters.n: The kingdom will be taken from those who reject him and given to a people who produce its fruit.

f.w: given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof

chapters.n: The stone image continues: those who stumble over Christ will be broken, and those on whom his judgment falls will be crushed.

f.w: whosoever shall fall on this stone

chapters.n: The chief priests and Pharisees realize the parables are about them.

f.w: they perceived that he spake of them

chapters.n: They want to arrest him on the spot but fear the crowds, who regard Jesus as a prophet.

f.w: they took him for a prophet

chapters.n: Still in the temple and still addressing the leaders, Jesus tells a third parable of judgment.

f.w: spake unto them again by parables

chapters.n: God’s kingdom is like a king throwing a wedding feast for his son. Scripture often pictures the messianic age as a great banquet.
Guests had been invited in advance, as was the custom; when the feast was ready, servants went to summon them. They refuse.

f.g: bidden = invited.

chapters.n: The king patiently sends more servants: the food is prepared, the best animals cooked — come!

f.g: Fattened calves or sheep, saved for special feasts.

chapters.n: The guests shrug it off and go about their business — farm and trade. Ordinary busyness can crowd out God’s invitation.

f.g: Treated it as unimportant.
Business, trade.

chapters.n: Others go further, mistreating and killing the king’s messengers — like the tenants of the previous parable.

f.g: entreated = treated; abused them shamefully.

chapters.n: The furious king sends troops, destroys the murderers, and burns their city — often seen as foreshadowing Jerusalem’s destruction by Rome in AD 70.
The feast is ready, but the invited guests proved unworthy.
So the king sends servants to the main roads to invite everyone they find.

f.g: Literally the places where roads leave the city — crossroads.

f.w: as many as ye shall find

chapters.n: They gather everyone, “both bad and good,” and the hall is full. The gospel invitation goes out to all.
The king comes to greet the guests and notices one man not wearing wedding clothes.

f.g: Proper festive clothing; many think the host may have supplied it. It symbolizes the righteousness required of those who accept the invitation.

chapters.n: Asked how he got in without the proper garment, the man has no answer.

f.g: Literally “muzzled” — he had no excuse.

chapters.n: The man is thrown out into the darkness. Accepting the invitation isn’t enough; we must also be changed and prepared.
Many receive God’s invitation, but few respond in a way that makes them chosen.

f.w: many are called, but few are chosen

chapters.n: The Pharisees now plot to trap Jesus with his own words.

f.g: Snare him, as a hunter traps a bird.

chapters.n: They send their students along with Herodians — normally their political rivals — opening with flattering praise of Jesus’s honesty and fearlessness.

f.g: Supporters of the Herod family and its cooperation with Rome.

f.w: thou regardest not the person of men
f.g: You aren’t swayed by anyone’s rank or status.

chapters.n: The trap: should Jews pay taxes to the Roman emperor? “Yes” angers the people; “no” is treason against Rome.

f.g: A Roman poll tax paid by subjects in Judea, bitterly resented.
The Roman emperor — at this time Tiberius.

chapters.n: Jesus sees through their scheme and calls them hypocrites.

f.g: Why are you testing me?

chapters.n: He asks for the coin used to pay the tax. They hand him a denarius.

f.g: A Roman denarius, a silver coin bearing the emperor’s portrait.

chapters.n: Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on it.

f.g: Inscription. Tiberius’s denarius named him son of the divine Augustus.

chapters.n: Brilliant answer: give Caesar what bears his image, and give God what bears God’s image — ourselves.

f.w: unto God the things that are God's

chapters.n: Amazed, they have nothing to say and leave.
Next come the Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, with a question meant to make the idea look ridiculous.

f.w: which say that there is no resurrection

chapters.n: They cite the law of levirate marriage: if a man dies childless, his brother marries the widow to continue his family line.

f.w: his brother shall marry his wife

f.g: Descendants.

chapters.n: Their story: seven brothers. The first marries and dies childless, leaving his wife to the next brother.

f.g: issue = children, offspring.

chapters.n: The same thing happens through all seven brothers.

f.g: An exaggerated hypothetical meant to produce an absurd result.

chapters.n: Finally the woman dies too.

f.w: last of all the woman died also
f.g: The setup is complete.

chapters.n: Their punch line: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be?

f.g: All seven were married to her.

chapters.n: Jesus says their mistake comes from not knowing either the scriptures or God’s power.

f.g: You are wrong, you go astray.

chapters.n: Resurrected beings don’t marry the way mortals do. Latter-day Saint teaching understands this to mean marriages are not performed after this life; eternal marriage must be sealed by proper authority now.

f.w: they neither marry, nor are given in marriage

chapters.n: Now Jesus answers their real question — is there a resurrection — from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

f.g: Concerning.

chapters.n: God told Moses “I am” (not “I was”) the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — long after they had died. They must still live to God.

f.w: I am the God of Abraham

chapters.n: The crowds are astonished by his teaching.
Hearing that the Sadducees were silenced, the Pharisees regroup.

f.g: Literally “muzzled” them.

chapters.n: One of them, an expert in the law, tests Jesus with a question.

f.g: A scribe — an expert in the law of Moses, not a courtroom attorney.

chapters.n: Which commandment is the greatest? Rabbis counted 613 commandments and debated which ones mattered most.
Jesus quotes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: love God with your whole heart, soul, and mind.

f.w: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God

chapters.n: This is the first and greatest commandment.
The second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. Love of God and love of others belong together.

f.w: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

chapters.n: All of scripture hangs on these two commandments, like a door hangs on its hinges.

f.w: hang all the law and the prophets

chapters.n: Now Jesus turns the tables and asks the gathered Pharisees a question.
Whose son is the Messiah? They give the standard answer: the son of David.
Then why, inspired by the Spirit, does David call the Messiah “Lord”?

f.g: Speaking by inspiration of the Holy Ghost.

chapters.n: He quotes Psalm 110, the Old Testament passage most quoted in the New: the LORD (God) tells David’s Lord (the Messiah) to sit at his right hand.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord

f.g: Conquered enemies were pictured under a king’s feet.

chapters.n: A father doesn’t call his son “Lord.” The answer: the Messiah is David’s descendant and also divine, the Son of God.
No one can answer, and from then on nobody dares to question him publicly. Next, Jesus will speak out against them.

f.g: durst = dared.

chapters.n: Jesus now speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the religious leaders. This is his final public teaching in the temple.

f.w: to the multitude, and to his disciples

chapters.n: The scribes and Pharisees act as official teachers of the law of Moses, as though seated in his chair.

f.g: A seat of teaching authority; ancient synagogues had a stone chair by this name.

chapters.n: So far as they teach the law, listen to them — but don’t copy their behavior, because they don’t practice what they preach.
They pile heavy religious rules on people but won’t lift a finger to help them carry the load.

f.g: Hard to carry.

chapters.n: Their religion is a performance. They make their scripture boxes extra wide and their tassels extra long to look especially devout.

f.g: Small leather boxes holding scripture passages, strapped to the forehead and arm during prayer.
The tassels on cloak corners commanded in the law.

chapters.n: They love the honored seats at banquets and the front seats in synagogues.

f.g: The places of honor at the table.
Synagogue seats facing the congregation.

chapters.n: They enjoy respectful public greetings and being called “Rabbi.”

f.g: Hebrew “my great one” — a title of honor for a teacher.

chapters.n: Disciples shouldn’t seek such titles. Christ is their one Teacher, and they are all equals.
Don’t give anyone the ultimate honor that belongs only to our Father in Heaven. Jesus targets status-seeking, not normal respect for parents.

f.w: one is your Father, which is in heaven

chapters.n: Christ alone is the final guide and leader.

f.g: Greek kathēgētēs — instructor, guide, leader.

chapters.n: Greatness in Christ’s kingdom is measured by service.
God reverses human pride: the self-promoting will be humbled, and the humble lifted up.

f.g: abased = brought low, humbled.

f.w: he that shall humble himself shall be exalted

chapters.n: The first of a series of woes. They shut the door of God’s kingdom — refusing to enter themselves and blocking others who want to.

f.g: An expression of grief and warning of judgment — the opposite of “blessed.”

f.w: ye shut up the kingdom of heaven

chapters.n: They cheat vulnerable widows out of their homes while making a show of long prayers. Their punishment will be greater. (Many ancient manuscripts lack this verse; Mark 12:40 has it.)

f.g: For show, as a cover.

chapters.n: They travel everywhere to win a single convert, then make that convert even more misguided than themselves.

f.g: compass = travel around.
A Gentile convert to Judaism.

chapters.n: They taught that oaths by the temple didn’t bind, but oaths by its gold did — clever loopholes for lying.

f.g: He is bound by his oath.

chapters.n: Which is greater — the gold, or the temple that makes the gold holy?

f.g: sanctify = make holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: They made the same hair-splitting distinction between swearing by the altar and by the offering on it.

f.w: the gift that is upon it
f.g: The sacrifice offered on the altar.

chapters.n: The altar is what makes the gift holy. Their reasoning was upside down.

f.w: the altar that sanctifieth the gift

chapters.n: An oath by the altar includes everything on it.

f.w: sweareth by it, and by all things thereon
f.g: There is no loophole.

chapters.n: An oath by the temple is ultimately an oath by God, who dwells there.
And swearing by heaven is swearing by God himself. Every oath involves God; honesty can’t be dodged.
They carefully tithe tiny garden herbs but neglect the weightier things — justice, mercy, faithfulness. Jesus says do both, but don’t lose the heart of the law.

f.g: Small kitchen herbs and spices; anise is likely dill.
judgment = justice; faith = faithfulness.

chapters.n: A comic picture: carefully straining a tiny gnat out of a drink while gulping down a whole camel. Both were unclean animals.

f.g: Strain out a gnat — people filtered wine through cloth to avoid swallowing unclean insects.

chapters.n: They clean the outside of cups and dishes but leave the inside full of greed and self-indulgence.

f.g: Robbery and lack of self-control.

chapters.n: Clean the inside first; a clean heart leads to genuinely clean outward conduct.

f.w: cleanse first that which is within

chapters.n: They’re like whitewashed tombs: bright and clean on the outside, full of decay inside. Tombs were whitewashed so people wouldn’t accidentally touch them and become unclean.

f.g: Tombs painted with lime, especially before Passover, to mark them.

chapters.n: Likewise, they look righteous to others but are full of hypocrisy and sin inside.
They build and decorate monuments to the prophets their ancestors killed.

f.g: Decorate the tombs.

chapters.n: They claim they would never have joined in killing the prophets.

f.g: Sharers, accomplices.

chapters.n: But by calling them “our fathers,” they admit their descent — and their actions show they share the same spirit.

f.g: You testify against yourselves.

chapters.n: Bitter irony: go ahead and finish what your ancestors started — a reference to the plot to kill Jesus.

f.w: Fill ye up then the measure
f.g: Complete the full amount of their guilt.

chapters.n: Jesus uses John the Baptist’s harsh words: snakes, offspring of vipers. How will they escape judgment?

f.g: Condemnation to Gehenna.

chapters.n: Jesus will send more messengers — prophets, wise men, and teachers — and they too will be persecuted and killed.
This generation will bear accountability for all the righteous blood shed, from the first murder (Abel) to Zacharias — the first and last murders in the Hebrew Bible’s order.

f.g: Most likely the priest Zechariah stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles is last in the Hebrew Bible); Joseph Smith taught it referred to John the Baptist’s father.

chapters.n: Judgment will fall on this very generation — fulfilled when Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70.
Jesus’s anger turns to heartbreak. Like a mother hen sheltering chicks, he longed to gather and protect Jerusalem’s people — but they refused.

f.w: as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings

chapters.n: Their “house” — likely the temple and the city — will be left abandoned and desolate.

f.w: your house is left unto you desolate

chapters.n: They won’t see him again until they welcome him with the words of Psalm 118 — pointing ahead to his Second Coming, when Israel will recognize him.

f.w: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord

chapters.n: Leaving the temple for the last time, Jesus’s disciples point out its impressive buildings. Herod the Great had expanded it into one of the ancient world’s grandest structures.

f.g: Some of Herod’s foundation stones weighed many tons; the work continued for decades.

chapters.n: Jesus shocks them: not one stone will be left standing on another. Roman armies fulfilled this in AD 70.

f.w: There shall not be left here one stone upon another

chapters.n: On the Mount of Olives, facing the temple, the disciples ask two questions: when will the temple fall, and what will signal his coming and the end of the world? This begins the Olivet Discourse.

f.g: The Joseph Smith Translation adds “or the destruction of the wicked.”

chapters.n: Jesus’s first concern is that they not be deceived.

f.w: Take heed that no man deceive you

chapters.n: Many will come claiming to be the Messiah and will mislead many people.
Wars and rumors of wars will come, but don’t panic — these alone don’t mean the end has arrived.
Nations will fight one another, and there will be famines, epidemics, and earthquakes in many places.

f.g: Plagues, epidemics.
divers = various.

chapters.n: These are only the beginning — like the first pains of childbirth before the new age is born.

f.g: Greek ōdin — birth pains.

chapters.n: Disciples will be persecuted, handed over, and killed, hated everywhere for bearing Christ’s name.

f.w: deliver you up to be afflicted

chapters.n: Many will fall away and turn on one another.

f.g: Stumble and fall away from faith.

chapters.n: False prophets will arise and lead many astray.
As wickedness increases, many people’s love will grow cold.

f.g: wax = grow, become.

chapters.n: Those who stay faithful to the end will be saved.

f.w: he that shall endure unto the end

chapters.n: Before the end, the gospel will be preached to all nations as a witness. Latter-day Saints see worldwide missionary work as part of this fulfillment.

f.w: this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world

chapters.n: Daniel’s “abomination of desolation” — a desecration of the holy place — signals disaster. Fulfilled when Rome defiled and destroyed the temple, it has a latter-day fulfillment too.

f.g: Something detestable that brings ruin, especially desecration of the sanctuary.

chapters.n: When that happens, those in Judea should flee to the mountains immediately. Early Christians reportedly fled to Pella before Jerusalem fell.
There will be no time to gather possessions. Someone on a flat rooftop should take the outside stairs and run.

f.g: Flat roofs were used as living space and often reached by outside stairs.

chapters.n: A worker in the field shouldn’t even go back for his cloak.

f.g: His outer cloak, often left at the field’s edge while working.

chapters.n: Jesus expresses compassion for pregnant women and nursing mothers, for whom fleeing would be especially hard.

f.g: Nursing mothers.

chapters.n: Pray that you won’t have to flee in winter, when roads flood, or on the Sabbath, when travel was limited and gates were shut.
The distress will be unmatched. Josephus describes horrific suffering during the Roman siege of Jerusalem.
If those days weren’t cut short, no one would survive; for the sake of God’s chosen, they will be shortened.

f.g: God’s chosen people — in JS—Matthew, “the elect according to the covenant.”

chapters.n: Don’t believe anyone who says the Messiah is here or there.
False Christs and prophets will perform impressive signs, almost able to deceive even God’s chosen.

f.w: if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect

chapters.n: Jesus has warned them in advance so they won’t be caught off guard.
Don’t go chasing rumors of a hidden Messiah in the desert or in secret rooms.

f.g: Inner rooms — a secret hiding place.

chapters.n: His real coming will be unmistakable — as visible as lightning flashing across the whole sky.

f.w: as the lightning cometh out of the east

chapters.n: Where a carcass lies, birds of prey gather — a proverb about inevitability. Joseph Smith’s translation applies it to the gathering of the elect from all the earth.

f.g: Probably vultures (the Greek word covers both).
carcase = carcass, dead body.

chapters.n: After the tribulation, the heavens themselves will be shaken — dramatic signs in sun, moon, and stars.

f.r: Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10, 31; D&C 45:42; D&C 88:87; Joseph Smith—Matthew 1:33

chapters.n: The sign of the Son of Man will appear, the nations will mourn, and all will see him coming on the clouds in power and glory.

f.w: coming in the clouds of heaven
all the tribes of the earth mourn

chapters.n: He will send angels with a great trumpet blast to gather his chosen from every direction.

f.w: a great sound of a trumpet

f.g: All four directions — the whole earth.

chapters.n: Learn from the fig tree: when its branches get tender and sprout leaves, you know summer is near.

f.w: a parable of the fig tree

chapters.n: In the same way, when these signs appear, his coming is close — right at the door.
“This generation” will see these things fulfilled. JS—Matthew clarifies it means the generation in which the signs are shown.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but Jesus’s words are absolutely certain.

f.w: my words shall not pass away

chapters.n: No one knows the exact day or hour — not even the angels. Only the Father knows. Date-setting is pointless; readiness is everything.

f.w: of that day and hour knoweth no man

chapters.n: His coming will be like the days of Noah.

f.g: Noe = Noah.

chapters.n: Before the Flood people went on with ordinary life — eating, drinking, marrying — right up until Noah entered the ark. The problem wasn’t daily life; it was ignoring God’s warning.
They didn’t realize what was happening until the flood swept them away. So it will be when the Son of Man comes.

f.w: knew not until the flood came

chapters.n: Two people will be working side by side in a field; one will be taken and the other left — a sudden separation.

f.w: the one shall be taken, and the other left

chapters.n: Two women grinding grain together at a hand mill — one taken, one left.

f.g: Women ground daily flour with a small stone hand mill, often in pairs.

chapters.n: So stay alert and ready, since you don’t know the hour of your Lord’s coming.

f.g: Stay awake, be alert.

chapters.n: If a homeowner knew when a thief would come, he would stay awake and keep his house from being broken into.

f.g: Here a period of the night, as in 14:25.
broken into — houses of mud brick could be dug through.

chapters.n: Be ready at all times; Christ will come when people least expect him.
A parable: who is the faithful, wise servant put in charge of his master’s household to give everyone food at the right time?

f.g: meat = food; in due season = at the proper time.

chapters.n: Blessed is the servant whom the master finds faithfully doing his job when he returns.
The faithful servant will be put in charge of all the master’s possessions.
But a wicked servant tells himself the master won’t be back for a long time.
So he abuses his fellow servants and joins the drunkards.

f.g: smite = strike, beat.

chapters.n: His master will show up on a day and hour he doesn’t expect.

f.w: when he looketh not for him

chapters.n: He will be severely punished and placed with the hypocrites, where there is weeping and bitter regret.

f.g: An image of harsh punishment — literally “cut in two.”

chapters.n: Continuing on the Mount of Olives, Jesus tells a parable about readiness. Ten young women, bridesmaids, wait with lamps to join the groom’s procession.

f.g: Unmarried young women, friends of the bride, who escorted the groom to the wedding feast.
Probably torches or small clay oil lamps that needed constant refueling.

chapters.n: All ten look alike from the outside — all invited, all waiting. The difference is preparation.

f.g: The word for “foolish” is Greek mōros, root of “moron.”

chapters.n: The foolish ones brought lamps but no extra oil.

f.g: Many see the oil as personal spiritual preparation — testimony, conversion, and the Holy Spirit.

chapters.n: The wise ones brought flasks of oil along with their lamps.

f.g: Small jars or flasks.

chapters.n: The groom is delayed, and all ten doze off. Sleeping isn’t the problem — being unprepared is.

f.g: tarried = delayed, was late.

chapters.n: At midnight comes the shout: the groom is coming! Christ’s return will come at an unexpected hour.
All ten wake up and trim their lamps to make them burn brightly.

f.g: Cut the wick and adjusted it so the lamp would burn well.

chapters.n: The foolish ones realize their lamps are going out and ask the wise for some oil.

f.g: Literally “are going out” — flickering and dying.

chapters.n: The wise can’t share — there isn’t enough. Some things, like personal faith and preparation, can’t be borrowed.

f.w: lest there be not enough for us and you

chapters.n: While they go to buy oil, the groom arrives. Those ready go in to the feast, and the door is shut.
The other five finally arrive and plead to be let in.
The groom says, “I don’t know you.” The JST reads “Ye know me not,” emphasizing that they had not truly come to know him.
The lesson: stay ready, for no one knows when the Son of Man will come.
A second parable: a man going on a long journey entrusts his property to his servants.
He gives five talents to one, two to another, and one to another, each according to ability. Even one talent was an enormous sum.

f.g: A talent was a large weight of silver — about 20 years of a laborer’s wages. Our English word “talent” (ability) comes from this parable.
several = individual, respective.

chapters.n: The first servant puts the money to work and doubles it.
The second likewise doubles his two talents.

f.g: His faithfulness matches the first servant’s, even though his amount is smaller.

chapters.n: The third digs a hole and buries the money — a common way to protect valuables, but it earns nothing.
After a long time the master returns and settles accounts with them.

f.g: A hint that Christ’s return may be later than some expect.
reckon = settle accounts.

chapters.n: The first servant reports that he has doubled the five talents.

f.w: I have gained beside them five talents more

chapters.n: The master praises him and promises far greater responsibility — and invites him into his own joy.

f.w: Well done, thou good and faithful servant
enter thou into the joy of thy lord

chapters.n: The second servant reports doubling his two talents.

f.w: I have gained two other talents
f.g: Same effort, different starting point.

chapters.n: He receives exactly the same praise as the first. God measures faithfulness, not the size of our gifts.
The third servant blames the master, calling him harsh and demanding — someone who profits from others’ work.

f.g: Harsh, severe.
strawed = scattered (seed).

chapters.n: Fear made him bury the talent. He returns it untouched, as if that is enough.
The master calls him wicked and lazy, using his own words against him: if he believed that, he should have acted accordingly.

f.g: slothful = lazy.

chapters.n: He could at least have deposited the money with bankers to earn interest.

f.g: Bankers, moneylenders.
usury = interest (not necessarily excessive here).

chapters.n: His talent is taken away and given to the servant who now has ten.

f.w: give it unto him which hath ten talents

chapters.n: Gifts we use grow; gifts we neglect are lost. This principle applies to talents, light, and truth.

f.w: unto every one that hath shall be given

chapters.n: The useless servant is cast into the outer darkness, full of regret.
The final scene of the discourse: the Son of Man coming in glory with all his angels to sit on his throne as King and Judge.
All nations are gathered before him, and he separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, which often grazed together by day.

f.w: as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats

chapters.n: The sheep go on his right, the place of honor and favor; the goats on his left.
The King invites the blessed to inherit the kingdom the Father prepared for them before the world was made.

f.w: prepared for you from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: He explains why: they fed him when he was hungry, gave him drink, and welcomed him as a stranger.

f.w: I was a stranger, and ye took me in

chapters.n: They clothed him, cared for him when sick, and visited him in prison.

f.w: I was sick, and ye visited me

chapters.n: The righteous are surprised: when did they ever see the Lord in need? They served without thinking they were doing anything remarkable.

f.w: when saw we thee an hungred
f.g: an hungred = hungry.

chapters.n: They continue to wonder when they welcomed or clothed him.

f.g: Here: poorly clothed, lacking adequate clothing.

chapters.n: Or when they visited him sick or in prison.
The King’s answer is one of the most important teachings in scripture: whatever we do for the least of his brothers and sisters, we do for him.

f.w: Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren

chapters.n: Those on his left are sent away into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels — not originally meant for humans.

f.g: In LDS understanding, “everlasting” describes God’s punishment, not necessarily its length.

chapters.n: They failed to feed or give drink to him in his need.

f.g: meat = food.

chapters.n: They didn’t welcome, clothe, or visit him. Their sin is neglect — what they failed to do.
They too are surprised, protesting that they never saw him in need. They didn’t recognize Christ in people around them.

f.g: athirst = thirsty.
Serve, care for.

chapters.n: Neglecting the least of these was neglecting Christ himself.

f.w: ye did it not to me

chapters.n: The two groups go to their separate destinies — punishment or eternal life. This ends Jesus’s last great discourse in Matthew.
Jesus finishes his final discourse. Matthew’s formula now says “all these sayings” — the teaching ministry is complete, and the story turns to his suffering.

f.w: when Jesus had finished all these sayings

chapters.n: Jesus knows exactly what is coming: Passover is two days away, and he will be handed over to be crucified. He goes forward willingly.

f.g: The annual festival remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, when a lamb was sacrificed.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the leaders meet at the residence of Caiaphas, the high priest.

f.g: High priest from about AD 18 to 36, son-in-law of the former high priest Annas.

chapters.n: They plot to arrest Jesus by stealth and have him killed.

f.g: subtilty = cunning, deceit, trickery.

chapters.n: They want to avoid the festival itself, fearing a riot among the huge Passover crowds who admired Jesus.

f.g: Jerusalem’s population swelled dramatically at Passover.

chapters.n: In Bethany, Jesus dines at the home of Simon the leper — likely someone Jesus had healed.
A woman — John identifies her as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus — pours very costly perfumed oil on Jesus’s head.

f.g: A sealed flask of soft stone; it was broken to pour out the contents.
Anointing the head recalls how kings were anointed.

chapters.n: The disciples are indignant at what they see as waste.

f.w: To what purpose is this waste?
f.g: John says Judas led this complaint.

chapters.n: They reason the perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Mark says it was worth over 300 denarii — about a year’s wages.
Jesus defends her: she has done a beautiful thing for him.

f.g: Done a beautiful, noble deed.

chapters.n: There will always be chances to help the poor, but only a little time left to honor him in person.

f.w: ye have the poor always with you

chapters.n: Her act anointed his body ahead of his burial. She seems to understand what the disciples don’t.

f.w: she did it for my burial

chapters.n: Jesus promises her act of devotion will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached — and it still is.

f.g: As a way of remembering her.

chapters.n: In sharp contrast to the woman’s generosity, Judas, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests.
Judas asks what they’ll pay to have Jesus handed over. They agree on thirty silver coins — the legal price of a slave.

f.g: Agreed, made a deal; or literally “weighed out.”

chapters.n: From then on Judas watches for a chance to betray Jesus quietly.
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: A seven-day festival joined to Passover, when no yeast was eaten.

chapters.n: Jesus sends them to a particular man in the city to arrange a room. He knows his “time” has arrived.

f.g: A certain person — left unnamed, perhaps to keep the location secret from Judas.

chapters.n: The disciples follow his directions and prepare the Passover.

f.g: Preparing the lamb, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and wine.

chapters.n: At evening Jesus reclines at the table with the Twelve.

f.g: Reclined — Passover was eaten reclining, as free people.

chapters.n: During the meal Jesus makes a devastating announcement: one of them will betray him.

f.w: one of you shall betray me

chapters.n: Deeply grieved, each asks, “Lord, is it I?” — humbly examining himself instead of accusing others.

f.g: The Greek form expects the answer “no” — “Surely not I, Lord?”

chapters.n: The betrayer is someone sharing the common dish with him — a close companion. Sharing a meal implied loyalty and friendship.

f.w: He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish

chapters.n: Jesus’s death fulfills scripture, yet the betrayer is still fully responsible for his choice.

f.w: as it is written of him
if he had not been born

chapters.n: Judas asks the same question, calling Jesus “Rabbi” rather than “Lord.” Jesus’s answer, “You have said it,” quietly confirms it.

f.g: Greek rhabbi — a teacher’s title, unlike the others’ “Lord.”
An idiom meaning “Yes — your words, not mine.”

chapters.n: Jesus takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to them: “This is my body.” This institutes the sacrament.

f.g: The JST adds that the bread is “in remembrance of my body.”

chapters.n: He takes the cup, gives thanks, and tells them all to drink from it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō.

chapters.n: The wine represents his blood, which seals a new covenant and is shed for the forgiveness of sins.

f.g: testament = covenant.
Forgiveness, release.

chapters.n: He won’t drink wine again until he drinks it new with them in his Father’s kingdom — a promise of future reunion.

f.w: until that day when I drink it new with you

chapters.n: They sing a hymn — traditionally the Hallel psalms closing the Passover — and go out to the Mount of Olives.

f.g: Probably part of Psalms 113–118, sung at Passover.

chapters.n: Jesus tells them they will all desert him that night, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the stricken shepherd.

f.g: Stumble, fall away.

chapters.n: But he promises that after rising, he will go ahead of them to Galilee — hope even amid the warning.

f.w: I will go before you into Galilee

chapters.n: Peter insists that even if everyone else falls away, he never will.

f.w: yet will I never be offended

chapters.n: Jesus foretells that before the rooster crows that very night, Peter will deny him three times.

f.g: Before dawn; “cockcrow” also named the watch from about midnight to 3 a.m.
thrice = three times.

chapters.n: Peter vows he would die rather than deny Jesus, and all the disciples say the same. Their love is sincere, but they don’t yet know their own weakness.

f.w: Though I should die with thee

chapters.n: They reach Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Jesus asks most of them to wait while he prays.

f.g: Aramaic for “oil press,” where olives were crushed for oil.

chapters.n: He takes Peter, James, and John further in, and begins to feel overwhelming sorrow and distress.

f.g: Deeply distressed, weighed down.

chapters.n: Jesus confides that his anguish is crushing him nearly to death, and asks them to stay awake with him.

f.w: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death

chapters.n: Falling to the ground, he prays: if possible, let this cup pass — yet your will, not mine. Here Jesus begins to take on himself the sins and suffering of all.

f.w: let this cup pass from me
not as I will, but as thou wilt
