chapters.n: Returning, he finds the disciples asleep and asks Peter, “Couldn’t you watch with me even one hour?”

f.w: could ye not watch with me one hour?

chapters.n: He urges them to watch and pray to resist temptation. Their spirit wants to do right, but the body is weak.

f.w: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak

chapters.n: He prays a second time, now accepting that he must drink the cup: “Thy will be done.”
Again he finds them asleep, unable to keep their eyes open.

f.g: Luke says they were sleeping for sorrow.

chapters.n: A third time he goes and prays the same prayer.
Returning, he tells them the hour has come; he is being handed over to sinners.

f.g: Possibly a question: “Are you still sleeping?”

chapters.n: “Get up, let’s go” — Jesus goes forward to meet his betrayer rather than fleeing.
Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests and elders.

f.g: staves = clubs, sticks.

chapters.n: Judas had arranged a signal: the one he kisses is Jesus. In the dark, they needed to be sure who to seize.

f.g: A kiss was a common greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

chapters.n: He goes straight up, greets Jesus, and kisses him — a sign of affection turned into betrayal.

f.g: A greeting, like “Greetings!”
The Greek implies an intense or prolonged kiss.

chapters.n: Jesus still calls Judas “friend” and asks him to do what he came for. Then they seize Jesus.

f.g: Greek hetairos — companion; also used in 20:13 and 22:12.
Possibly “Do what you came to do.”

chapters.n: One disciple — John names him as Peter — draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant.

f.g: John names the servant Malchus; Luke says Jesus healed the ear.

chapters.n: Jesus tells him to put the sword away. Violence only breeds more violence; his kingdom is not won that way.

f.w: all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword

chapters.n: If Jesus wanted rescue, his Father would instantly send more than twelve legions of angels. He goes to the cross by choice.

f.g: A Roman legion was about 6,000 soldiers — over 70,000 angels.

chapters.n: But then the scriptures about the Messiah’s suffering wouldn’t be fulfilled.
Jesus points out the absurdity: they come with weapons as if for a bandit, yet he taught openly in the temple every day.

f.g: As against a robber or rebel.

chapters.n: This too fulfills the prophets. Then all the disciples abandon him and run, just as he foretold.

f.w: all the disciples forsook him, and fled

chapters.n: Jesus is taken to Caiaphas, where the Jewish leaders have gathered at night.

f.g: John notes a preliminary hearing before Annas first.

chapters.n: Peter follows at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and sits with the guards to see what happens.

f.g: To see how it would turn out.

chapters.n: The council seeks false testimony to justify a death sentence — a trial with the verdict decided beforehand.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member supreme Jewish council.

chapters.n: Many false witnesses come forward, but their stories don’t agree. The law required witnesses to agree. Finally two come forward.
They twist Jesus’s earlier words about destroying and rebuilding the temple. He had been speaking of his body.

f.w: I am able to destroy the temple of God

chapters.n: The high priest demands that Jesus respond to the charges.
Jesus stays silent, as Isaiah foretold. Then Caiaphas puts him under solemn oath: is he the Christ, the Son of God?

f.g: I put you under oath.

chapters.n: Jesus affirms it, then declares they will see him at God’s right hand and coming on the clouds — combining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7.

f.g: “Power” was a reverent substitute for God’s name.

chapters.n: The high priest tears his robes — a ritual sign of horror at blasphemy — and declares no more witnesses are needed.

f.g: rent = tore.

chapters.n: The council pronounces him deserving of death.
They spit in his face and beat him — the Judge of all being judged by men.

f.g: buffeted = struck with fists.

chapters.n: Blindfolded (as Mark notes), Jesus is mocked: “Prophesy — who hit you?”
Outside in the courtyard, a servant girl says Peter was with Jesus of Galilee.

f.g: without = outside.
A young servant girl.

chapters.n: Peter denies it in front of everyone, pretending not to understand.

f.w: I know not what thou sayest

chapters.n: At the gateway, another girl identifies him as a follower of Jesus of Nazareth.

f.g: The gateway or entrance passage.

chapters.n: Peter denies again, this time with an oath: “I don’t know the man.”
Bystanders say his Galilean accent gives him away.

f.g: bewrayeth = betrays, reveals.
His Galilean accent was distinct from Judean speech.

chapters.n: Peter calls down curses and swears he doesn’t know Jesus — and immediately the rooster crows.

f.g: To invoke a curse on himself if lying, and to take oaths.

chapters.n: Remembering Jesus’s words, Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. His sorrow leads to repentance; he will become a mighty witness.
At dawn the council meets formally to confirm the death sentence, since night trials were considered improper.
Under Roman rule the Jewish council couldn’t carry out executions, so they bind Jesus and hand him over to Pilate, the Roman governor.

f.g: Roman governor (prefect) of Judea about AD 26–36; an inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

chapters.n: Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas is overcome with remorse and tries to return the thirty silver coins.

f.g: Greek metamelomai — felt regret or remorse, a different word from the usual one for repentance.

chapters.n: Judas admits he has betrayed innocent blood. The leaders coldly reply, “That’s your problem.”

f.g: That’s your concern, not ours.

chapters.n: He throws the money into the temple and goes off and hangs himself — a tragic end of despair.
The chief priests, who paid the blood money, now scruple over putting it in the temple treasury — a striking picture of the hypocrisy Jesus condemned.

f.g: Greek korbanas — the temple treasury.

chapters.n: They use it to buy a potter’s field as a cemetery for foreigners who died in Jerusalem.

f.g: Perhaps a field where potters dug clay, no longer useful for farming.
Foreigners, visitors to Jerusalem.

chapters.n: The place became known as the Field of Blood.

f.g: Aramaic Akeldama.

chapters.n: Matthew sees prophecy fulfilled. The wording is mostly from Zechariah, combined with themes from Jeremiah about a potter and a purchased field.

f.g: Jeremy = Jeremiah.

chapters.n: The silver paid for the potter’s field, as the Lord had directed — the price at which Israel valued its Shepherd.
Pilate asks if Jesus is the King of the Jews — a political charge Rome would take seriously. Jesus answers, “You say so.”

f.w: Art thou the King of the Jews?

f.g: A guarded yes — true, but not in the sense you mean.

chapters.n: To the many accusations from the priests and elders, Jesus makes no reply.
Pilate presses him: doesn’t he hear all these charges?

f.w: how many things they witness against thee

chapters.n: Jesus doesn’t answer even one charge, and Pilate is amazed. Defendants normally fought for their lives.
It was the governor’s custom to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd at Passover.

f.g: was wont = was accustomed, usually did.

chapters.n: A notorious prisoner named Barabbas was being held — Mark and Luke say for rebellion and murder.

f.g: Aramaic “son of the father” — an ironic contrast with Jesus, the true Son of the Father.
Notorious, well known.

chapters.n: Pilate offers a choice: Barabbas or Jesus, “called Christ.”

f.w: Whom will ye that I release unto you?

chapters.n: Pilate realizes the leaders handed Jesus over out of envy, not justice.
While Pilate sits in judgment, his wife sends an urgent warning: have nothing to do with this righteous man; she has suffered in a dream about him.

f.g: Greek bēma — the official platform where a magistrate gave verdicts.

chapters.n: The leaders persuade the crowd to demand Barabbas and Jesus’s death.
Asked again which one to release, they shout, “Barabbas!”

f.g: Which of the two.

chapters.n: “Then what should I do with Jesus?” They all cry, “Crucify him!”
Pilate asks what crime he has committed; they only shout louder.
Fearing a riot, Pilate washes his hands publicly and declares himself innocent. But washing his hands cannot erase his responsibility.

f.g: A symbolic act of disclaiming guilt, also known in Jewish law.
A riot, uproar.

chapters.n: The crowd cries that the blood be on them and their children. Tragically, this verse was later misused to blame all Jews — a reading scripture and the Church reject; each person answers for his own sins.

f.w: His blood be on us, and on our children

chapters.n: Pilate frees Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands him over to be crucified. Roman scourging with metal- or bone-tipped whips was brutal and sometimes fatal.

f.g: Whipped with a flagrum, a whip of leather straps weighted with bits of metal or bone.

chapters.n: The soldiers take Jesus into the governor’s headquarters and gather the whole cohort.

f.g: The praetorium — the governor’s official residence.
A cohort, up to 600 soldiers.

chapters.n: They strip him and throw a red military cloak over him, mocking him as a king in royal colors.

f.g: Probably a soldier’s red cloak, imitating royal purple.

chapters.n: They twist thorns into a crown, put a reed in his hand as a scepter, and kneel in mock homage: “Hail, King of the Jews!”

f.g: plaited = woven, braided.
Thorns are a symbol of the curse of the Fall; Christ wears them as he overcomes it.

chapters.n: They spit on him and beat him on the head with the reed.
Done mocking, they put his own clothes back on him and lead him out to be crucified.

f.w: led him away to crucify him

chapters.n: Weakened by the beating, Jesus can’t carry the cross beam. Soldiers force Simon of Cyrene, a passerby, to carry it.

f.g: A city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a large Jewish community.
Roman soldiers could legally force civilians into service.

chapters.n: They reach Golgotha, “the place of a skull,” just outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.g: Aramaic for “skull”; Latin Calvaria gives us “Calvary.”

chapters.n: They offer him wine mixed with something bitter, probably a painkiller. He tastes it but refuses, choosing to face his suffering fully conscious.

f.g: Sour wine.
A bitter substance; Mark says myrrh.

chapters.n: They crucify him and gamble for his clothing — fulfilling Psalm 22.

f.g: Clothing; John says a seamless inner tunic.

chapters.n: The soldiers sit down to guard him until he dies.

f.g: Guarded him, to prevent any rescue.

chapters.n: Above his head is posted the charge: “This is Jesus the King of the Jews.” Meant as mockery, it is true.

f.w: THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS
f.g: John says it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.

chapters.n: Two criminals are crucified with him, one on each side — he is “numbered with the transgressors.”

f.g: Probably bandits or rebels (Greek lēstai).

f.w: one on the right hand, and another on the left

chapters.n: People passing by on the road hurl insults and shake their heads in scorn.

f.g: Insulted, abused.

chapters.n: They twist his words about the temple and taunt him to save himself — echoing Satan’s “If thou be the Son of God” in the wilderness.

f.w: If thou be the Son of God

chapters.n: The chief priests, scribes, and elders join in the mockery.
“He saved others; he can’t save himself.” Deep irony: it is precisely by not saving himself that he saves others.

f.w: He saved others; himself he cannot save

chapters.n: They taunt him with words from Psalm 22, unknowingly fulfilling the very psalm that describes his suffering.

f.w: He trusted in God; let him deliver him now

chapters.n: Even the two crucified with him join the insults. Luke records that one later repented.

f.w: cast the same in his teeth
f.g: Taunted him in the same way.

chapters.n: From noon until 3 p.m. darkness covers the land. In the Americas, the Book of Mormon records three days of darkness at his death.

f.g: About noon; the ninth hour is about 3 p.m.

chapters.n: Jesus cries out the opening words of Psalm 22 in Aramaic. Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the Father withdrew his sustaining presence so the Son could finish the Atonement alone.

f.g: Abandoned, left alone.

chapters.n: Some bystanders mishear “Eli” as a call for Elijah, whom many believed would come to help the righteous in distress.

f.g: Elias = Elijah.

chapters.n: Someone runs to give him sour wine on a sponge lifted on a reed.

f.g: Cheap sour wine, the common drink of soldiers.

chapters.n: Others say, “Wait — let’s see if Elijah comes to rescue him.”

f.g: Leave him alone, wait.

chapters.n: Jesus cries out again with a loud voice and gives up his spirit. He doesn’t simply die — he voluntarily yields his life.

f.g: ghost = spirit. He released his spirit.

chapters.n: The temple veil, which separated the Holy of Holies from the rest of the temple, tears from top to bottom — as if by God’s hand. Through Christ the way into God’s presence is opened.

f.g: A heavy curtain before the Holy of Holies, where only the high priest entered once a year.

chapters.n: Tombs open, and many righteous people who had died are raised.

f.g: Righteous people who had died — death pictured as sleep.

chapters.n: After Jesus’s resurrection they come out of the tombs, enter Jerusalem, and appear to many. Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection.
The Roman centurion and soldiers on guard, seeing the earthquake and all that happened, are terrified and confess: “Truly this was the Son of God.” Gentiles recognize what the leaders denied.

f.w: Truly this was the Son of God

chapters.n: Many women who had followed and supported Jesus from Galilee watch from a distance. They stay when the male disciples have fled.

f.g: Serving and supporting him, including financially.

chapters.n: Matthew names some of them: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of James and John.

f.g: From Magdala on the Sea of Galilee; Jesus had cast seven devils out of her.

chapters.n: As evening approaches, Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy secret disciple and council member, steps forward. Burial was needed before the Sabbath began at sunset.

f.g: A town in Judea, perhaps the Old Testament Ramah.

chapters.n: Joseph boldly asks Pilate for Jesus’s body, and Pilate grants it.

f.g: Crucified criminals were often left unburied; asking was a risky act of loyalty.

chapters.n: Joseph wraps the body in clean linen. John adds that Nicodemus brought spices.
He lays Jesus in his own new tomb cut into rock and rolls a large stone across the entrance.

f.g: Such tombs were cut into hillsides; the stone was often a large disc rolled in a channel.
sepulchre = tomb.

chapters.n: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit facing the tomb. They know exactly where Jesus was laid — important for the resurrection morning.

f.g: Opposite, facing.

chapters.n: The next day — the Sabbath — the chief priests and Pharisees go to Pilate.

f.g: Friday, the day to prepare for the Sabbath.

chapters.n: They remember Jesus said he would rise after three days. Ironically, his enemies remember his promise better than his disciples.

f.w: After three days I will rise again

f.g: Impostor.

chapters.n: They ask for the tomb to be secured so the disciples can’t steal the body and claim a resurrection.

f.g: Made secure.

f.w: the last error shall be worse than the first
f.g: This deception would be worse than his claim to be Messiah.

chapters.n: Pilate tells them to use their own guard and secure it as best they can.

f.g: Either “You have your own guard” (temple police) or “Take a guard” (Roman soldiers).

chapters.n: They seal the stone and post guards. Their precautions will only make the empty tomb more certain evidence.

f.g: A cord fixed with wax or clay seal across the stone, so tampering would show.

chapters.n: After the Sabbath, at dawn on Sunday, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to see the tomb. Sunday became the Lord’s Day because of this morning.

f.w: the first day of the week

f.g: Probably Mary the mother of James and Joses.

chapters.n: A great earthquake strikes as an angel of the Lord descends, rolls the stone away, and sits on it. The stone is moved not to let Jesus out, but to let witnesses in.
The angel’s appearance blazes like lightning, his clothing white as snow — the brilliance of heavenly glory.

f.g: countenance = face, appearance.

chapters.n: The guards shake with fear and collapse like dead men. The soldiers posted to keep a dead man in look dead themselves.

f.g: The guards.

chapters.n: The angel comforts the women: don’t be afraid. He knows they are looking for Jesus who was crucified.
The central declaration of the Christian faith: “He is not here: for he is risen, as he said.” The women are invited to see the empty place for themselves.

f.w: he is risen, as he said
Come, see the place where the Lord lay

chapters.n: They are sent to tell the disciples that Jesus has risen and will meet them in Galilee. These women become the first messengers of the Resurrection.

f.w: he goeth before you into Galilee

chapters.n: They hurry from the tomb, filled with both fear and great joy, running to tell the disciples.

f.g: Awe and joy together — a natural response to the holy.

chapters.n: On the way, the risen Jesus himself meets them. They grasp his feet and worship him — touching a real, physical, resurrected body.

f.g: A greeting, literally “Rejoice!”

chapters.n: Jesus repeats the message, tenderly calling the disciples who abandoned him “my brethren.” He has not given up on them.
Meanwhile some of the guards report everything to the chief priests.

f.g: Reported to them.

chapters.n: The leaders meet and decide to bribe the soldiers with a large sum of money.

f.g: A large amount of silver — ironically paid again to suppress the truth about Jesus.

chapters.n: The cover story: the disciples stole the body while the guards slept. It is a weak story — how would sleeping guards know who took it?

f.w: stole him away while we slept

chapters.n: Sleeping on duty could mean death for a Roman soldier, so the leaders promise to protect them if Pilate hears.

f.g: Keep you out of trouble.

chapters.n: The soldiers take the money and spread the story, which Matthew says was still circulating when he wrote.

f.g: Until the time Matthew wrote his Gospel, likely a few decades later.

chapters.n: The eleven apostles — Judas is gone — go to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus told them to meet him.

f.g: Mountains frame Jesus’s ministry in Matthew: temptation, sermon, transfiguration, and now commission.

chapters.n: When they see him they worship him, though some hesitate. Matthew honestly records that faith sometimes grows gradually.

f.g: Greek distazō — to waver or hesitate, the word used of Peter on the water.

chapters.n: Jesus comes near and declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

f.w: All power is given unto me

chapters.n: The Great Commission: go to all nations — no longer only Israel — making disciples and baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

f.g: Literally “make disciples of all nations.”

f.w: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: They must teach people to live all he has commanded. Matthew ends with a promise: “I am with you always.” The Gospel that began with “God with us” ends with Christ remaining with his disciples.

f.g: The end of the age — the JST and JS—Matthew render similar phrases as “the destruction of the wicked.”
